• Configure the OS and rebind drivers;
  • Deploy the GPU Operator in vm-passthrough mode;
  • Configure the Kubevirt CRD to set your GPUs as permitted devices.

items.title: vGPU
items.text:
• Similar to VM-Passthrough, but includes the building and hosting of your own NVIDIA vGPU image; requires an NVIDIA Enterprise account with a subscription and license.
  • Support for the Talos operating system is unknown; this section is still in development.

items.title: Step 1: Include NVIDIA drivers in Talos
items.text:
1. Include the following 2 system extensions in your Talos image:

    • nvidia-open-gpu-kernel-modules
    • nvidia-container-toolkit

    You can do so either during installation, or through an Image Factory schematic upgrade.

  2. Apply this patch to your GPU node's Talos machine configuration: 

    # Talos machine configuration patch
machine:
  kernel:
    modules:
      - name: nvidia
      - name: nvidia_uvm
      - name: nvidia_drm
      - name: nvidia_modeset
  sysctls:
    net.core.bpf_jit_harden: 1

items.title: Step 2: Deploy the NVIDIA k8s-device-plugin
items.text:
1. Create a RuntimeClass that will allow pods to use the Talos NVIDIA extensions: 
    apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: nvidia
handler: nvidia
  2. Add the NVIDIA Device Plugin repository and update it: 
    helm repo add nvdp https://nvidia.github.io/k8s-device-plugin
helm repo update
  3. Install the NVIDIA Device Plugin: 
    helm install nvidia-device-plugin nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin \
  --set=runtimeClassName=nvidia

Your GPU hardware should now be visible inside your Kubernetes cluster in the form of allocatable nvidia.com/gpu resources.

You can test the RuntimeClass by running the following CUDA test pod: 

kubectl run \
  nvidia-test \
  --restart=Never \
  -ti --rm \
  --image nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/cuda-sample:vectoradd-cuda12.5.0 \
  --overrides '{"spec": {"runtimeClassName": "nvidia"}}' \
  nvidia-smi

items.title: Step 1: Configure the Talos OS
items.text:
• Enable IOMMU and SVM Mode in the BIOS:
    • On an AMD CPU:
      • Advanced > AMD CBS > NBIO Common Options > IOMMU/Security > Enable
      • Advanced > CPU Configuration > SVM Mode > Enable
  • Set the iommu=pt kernel parameter, either during installation or through an Image Factory schematic upgrade. Get the image either:
    • From the web UI, following the on-screen instructions : Talos Image Factory
    • Or from the terminal:
      • Create a customization.yaml schematic file containing your extra kernel arguments: 
        customization:
  extraKernelArgs:
    - iommu=pt
      • Query the Image Factory to get an ID for your customization: 
        curl -X POST --data-binary @customization.yaml https://factory.talos.dev/schematics
# Returns a schematic ID
    • Then apply the image through an upgrade: 
      talosctl --talosconfig talosconfig -n <node-IP> upgrade --image factory.talos.dev/metal-installer/<schematic-ID>:<Talos-version>
    • Patch your node's machine configuration to include the correct image: 
      # Talos machine configuration patch
machine:
  install:
    image: factory.talos.dev/metal-installer/<schematic-ID>:<Talos-version>

items.title: Step 2: Rebind all GPU devices to the vfio-pci driver
items.text:
1. List all NVIDIA GPU PCI devices and note their IDs down: 
    talosctl --talosconfig talosconfig -n <node-IP> get pcidevices | grep NVIDIA
  2. Create a patch file containing a PCIDriverRebindConfig for each GPU device, using their ID as name: 
    apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: PCIDriverRebindConfig
name: 0000:01:00.0
targetDriver: vfio-pci
---
apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: PCIDriverRebindConfig
name: 0000:11:00.0
targetDriver: vfio-pci
# etc...
  3. Include the following modules in the node's machine configuration: 
    # Talos machine configuration patch
machine:
  kernel:
    modules:
      - name: vfio_pci
      - name: vfio_iommu_type1
  4. Apply both patches to the node.

items.title: Step 3: Deploy the NVIDIA gpu-operator
items.text:
1. Label your GPU node for vm-passthrough mode: 
    kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite nvidia.com/gpu.workload.config=vm-passthrough
  2. Create the gpu-operator namespace and set its Pod Security to privileged: 
    kubectl create ns gpu-operator
kubectl label --overwrite ns gpu-operator pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged
  3. Add the NVIDIA Helm repository and update it: 
    helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia
helm repo update
  4. Install the GPU Operator: 
    helm upgrade --wait --install -n gpu-operator gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator \
  --set sandboxWorkloads.enabled=true \
  --set sandboxWorkloads.defaultWorkload=vm-passthrough \
  --set driver.enabled=false \
  --set toolkit.enabled=false \
  --set devicePlugin.enabled=false

items.title: Step 4: Configure Kubevirt
items.text:
Edit the Kubevirt CRD to add the following feature gates and permitted host devices: 

spec:
  configuration:
    developerConfiguration:
      featureGates:
      - GPU
      - DisableMDEVConfiguration
    permittedHostDevices:
      pciHostDevices:
      - externalResourceProvider: true
        pciVendorSelector: "10DE:2BB5"
        resourceName: "nvidia.com/GB202GL_RTX_PRO_6000_BLACKWELL_SERVER_EDITION"

Read more about the different fields in the official Kubevirt documentation.

You can now give GPUs to your VMs. Proceed with installing the necessary drivers inside your VM to take full advantage of your GPU devices.

About live-migration

Bear in mind that Kubevirt VMs using PCI host devices (in our case, passthrough GPUs) cannot be live-migrated.

items.title: 3. Talos with vGPU workloads
items.text: NVIDIA vGPU support for the Talos operating system is unknown; this section is still in development.

items.title: Relevant documentation
items.text: Talos documentation: NVIDIA GPU (OSS drivers) (v1.12) NVIDIA documentation: Installing the NVIDIA GPU Operator (v26.7)

items.title: Manual OS installation
items.text:
This guide covers installing Talos Linux on your servers and bootstrapping a Kubernetes cluster by hand, using talosctl. Use this path when you already have physical or virtual machines ready and want full control over the Talos machine configuration before handing the cluster to Superphenix.

Each command is shown for Linux and Windows. On Windows, use PowerShell.

For the automated alternative, see Automated OS installation.

For the installation of Talos Linux on GPU nodes, see Installing GPU Nodes.

items.title: When to use this path
items.text:
• First lab or single-AZ deployment: fastest way to get a working cluster on a small node count (for example 3 nodes in hyperconverged mode).
  • Management on an AZ: the management cluster must be a pre-existing Talos cluster before you install the superphenix-operator Helm chart.
  • Bring your own cluster: you manage Talos upgrades, machine configs, and node lifecycle yourself; Superphenix connects to the cluster via a Cluster resource with connection.mode: Local or Remote.

Official support scope

Superphenix is only officially supported on Talos. Use Talos 1.12.6 or older: newer versions hit a Linux kernel bug that breaks the SDN.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Before you start, confirm:

  • Hardware and network meet the profile for your topology: see Hardware requirements and Network requirements.
  • Deployment topology is chosen (hyperconverged vs decoupled, management in vs out): see Deployment topology.
  • talosctl (CLI reference) and kubectl on your workstation.
  • Talos 1.12.6 or older installer media (ISO, PXE, or disk image).
  • Servers can reach each other on the cluster VLAN and your workstation can reach each node on the Talos API port during bootstrap.

items.title: Installation overview
items.text:
1. Generate Talos machine configuration for your cluster endpoint.
  2. Boot each node from the Talos installer (ISO, PXE, or disk image).
  3. Apply machine configs to every node.
  4. Bootstrap etcd on the first control-plane node.
  5. Retrieve the kubeconfig and verify the Kubernetes API.
  6. Continue with Installing inside an AZ on this cluster (or register it as a remote cluster from your management plane).

items.title: Step 1: Generate cluster configuration
items.text:
Pick a stable Kubernetes API endpoint (VIP, load balancer, or first control-plane IP) and generate configs:

LinuxWindows 
talosctl gen config spx-cluster https://<api-endpoint>:6443

talosctl gen config spx-cluster "https://<api-endpoint>:6443"

This produces controlplane.yaml, worker.yaml, and talosconfig. Edit the generated files before you apply them.

Set node hostnames, disk selectors, and addressing to match your hardware. Superphenix installs the CNI and CoreDNS itself, so those must be disabled in Talos. Every node also needs the containerd and kernel settings below, plus an external interface with the same name on every node. Control-plane configs must enable MutatingAdmissionPolicy.

Edit controlplane.yaml (and worker.yaml if you use dedicated workers) with at least:

machine:
  files:
    - content: |
        [plugins]
          [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
            device_ownership_from_security_context = true
          [plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime"]
            device_ownership_from_security_context = true
      path: /etc/cri/conf.d/20-customization.part
      op: create
  kernel:
    modules:
      - name: openvswitch
  network:
    interfaces:
      - interface: ext0 # same name on every node (NIC, bond, or VLAN)
        dhcp: true
        routes:
          - network: 0.0.0.0/0
            gateway: 192.168.1.1 # your default gateway

cluster:
  network:
    cni:
      name: none
  coreDNS:
    disabled: true
  controllerManager:
    extraArgs:
      feature-gates: "MutatingAdmissionPolicy=true"
  apiServer:
    extraArgs:
      feature-gates: "MutatingAdmissionPolicy=true"
      runtime-config: "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1=true"

For a small hyperconverged lab with only control-plane nodes, also set cluster.allowSchedulingOnControlPlanes: true so Superphenix workloads can run on those nodes. Dedicated workers do not need that flag or the controllerManager / apiServer extraArgs; apply the same machine and cluster.network / coreDNS settings in worker.yaml.

Replace ext0, DHCP vs static addressing, and the default gateway to match your network. Keep the interface name identical on every node.

Same external interface name on every node

The external interface must have the same name on every node (ext0 here). Superphenix uses that name cluster-wide. If kernel names differ, append a LinkAliasConfig per node (physical NICs only; name bonds and VLANs yourself). Keep name: ext0 identical; change only the MAC:

---
apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: LinkAliasConfig
name: ext0
selector:
  match: mac(link.permanent_addr) == "00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e" # this node's NIC MAC

Do not use kernel-style alias names (eth0, ens3, enp0s31f6, …).

Official reference: Talos Getting Started.

items.title: Step 2: Boot the nodes
items.text:
Install Talos 1.12.6 or older on each server using one of:

  • ISO: boot from the Talos installer image and install to disk.
  • PXE: network boot for repeatable datacenter provisioning.
  • Image: flash a prepared disk image when you manage imaging outside Talos.

Each node should come up in maintenance mode and expose the Talos API on its management/cluster interface.

items.title: Step 3: Apply machine configuration
items.text:
Apply the control-plane config to every control-plane node (repeat for each node IP):

LinuxWindows 
talosctl apply-config --insecure --nodes <node-ip> --file controlplane.yaml

talosctl apply-config --insecure --nodes "<node-ip>" --file controlplane.yaml

If you use dedicated workers, apply worker.yaml to worker nodes instead.

items.title: Step 4: Bootstrap etcd
items.text:
From one control-plane node only, bootstrap the cluster:

LinuxWindows 
talosctl bootstrap --nodes <first-control-plane-ip>

TALOSCONFIG applies to the current PowerShell session only. Set it again in each new window.

$env:TALOSCONFIG = (Resolve-Path "talosconfig").Path
talosctl bootstrap --nodes "<first-control-plane-ip>"

Wait until the Kubernetes API responds on https://<api-endpoint>:6443.

items.title: Step 5: Verify the cluster
items.text:
Fetch kubeconfig and confirm nodes are ready:

LinuxWindows 
talosctl kubeconfig .
kubectl get nodes

TALOSCONFIG and KUBECONFIG apply to the current PowerShell session only. Set them again in each new window.

$env:TALOSCONFIG = (Resolve-Path "talosconfig").Path
talosctl kubeconfig .
$env:KUBECONFIG = (Resolve-Path "kubeconfig").Path
kubectl get nodes

All control-plane (and worker, if any) nodes should report Ready before you install Superphenix.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Install the operator: Installing inside an AZ or Installing outside an AZ.
  • Define your AZ: Configure a cluster.

items.title: Accessing Superphenix
items.text:
After Superphenix is deployed, use the web console for day-to-day resource management, ArgoCD to monitor the platform deployment, and the cluster toolbox for kubectl, Helm, and k9s on every managed cluster.

Administration UI in development

We are working on a dedicated administration UI. Until it is available, use Argo CD and kubectl/k9s from the cluster toolbox to monitor and troubleshoot the platform.

You need:

  • Network access to the console and ArgoCD hostnames configured during installation.
  • A working kubectl context for the management cluster, to retrieve the initial ArgoCD password and to open the cluster toolbox.

items.title: Open the web console
items.text:
Open the URL configured for the Superphenix console, for example:

https://console.example.org

The URL redirects you to the console login page. By default, self-service registration is enabled: anyone who can reach the page can create an account and sign in. Validating users manually holds new accounts until an administrator activates them.

Secure public deployments

Restrict network access to the console if you do not want to allow public registration. Mail, second factors, and super-admins are covered in Sending emails, MFA and recovery, and Setting super-admins.

After signing in, use the console to create and manage tenant resources such as virtual machines, networks, and storage.

items.title: Open ArgoCD
items.text:
Open the ArgoCD hostname configured during installation, for example:

https://argocd.example.org

Sign in with the username admin. Retrieve the generated initial password from the management cluster:

kubectl --namespace superphenix-system get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
  --output jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
echo

Note

If ArgoCD was installed in a different namespace, replace argocd in the command with that namespace.

Change the initial password after your first login.

items.title: Use the cluster toolbox
items.text:
The Superphenix operator can deploy an optional toolbox on the management cluster. The toolbox is a single shell from which administrators access every Kubernetes cluster managed by the operator.

It includes kubectl, Helm, k9s, and common troubleshooting utilities. The operator builds an aggregated kubeconfig from the connection details of the managed Cluster resources and mounts it in the toolbox.

items.title: Enable the toolbox
items.text:
The toolbox is disabled by default. Enable it in the Helm values of the superphenix-operator:

toolbox:
  enabled: true

Apply the values when installing or upgrading the operator. Confirm that the toolbox is ready:

kubectl --namespace superphenix-system \
  rollout status deployment/superphenix-toolbox

items.title: Open a toolbox shell
items.text:
From the management cluster, run:

kubectl --namespace superphenix-system exec --stdin --tty \
  deployment/superphenix-toolbox -- bash

The mounted kubeconfig is linked automatically to ~/.kube/config, so the included Kubernetes tools use it without additional configuration.

List the available contexts:

kubectl config get-contexts

Each context is named after its Superphenix Cluster resource. Select a cluster and verify access:

kubectl config use-context <cluster-name>
kubectl get nodes

You can then use kubectl, Helm, or k9s against the selected cluster:

helm list --all-namespaces
k9s

items.title: Kubeconfig updates
items.text:
The operator maintains the superphenix-toolbox-kubeconfig Secret from the connection configuration of all managed clusters. Kubernetes refreshes the mounted Secret when the operator updates it, so the toolbox receives credential and connection changes without being redeployed.

Run kubectl config get-contexts again after adding, removing, or changing a managed cluster.

Administrative access

The toolbox kubeconfig contains credentials for every cluster managed by the operator. Anyone who can execute commands in the toolbox or read the superphenix-toolbox-kubeconfig Secret can use those credentials. Restrict pod execution and Secret access in the superphenix-system namespace to platform administrators.

items.title: Check the toolbox
items.text:
Check the toolbox pod and its events:

kubectl --namespace superphenix-system get pods \
  --selector app.kubernetes.io/component=toolbox
kubectl --namespace superphenix-system describe \
  deployment/superphenix-toolbox

Confirm that the aggregated kubeconfig exists:

kubectl --namespace superphenix-system get \
  secret/superphenix-toolbox-kubeconfig

If a cluster is missing, inspect its Cluster resource and referenced connection Secret. Only clusters with valid local or remote connection configuration are added to the aggregated kubeconfig.

items.title: Monitor deployment and synchronization
items.text:
ArgoCD is the primary place to follow Superphenix deployment activity. The applications shown there represent the platform components managed through GitOps.

Use ArgoCD to:

  • Check whether applications are Synced or OutOfSync.
  • Check whether applications and their resources are Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, or Missing.
  • Inspect synchronization history and failed sync operations.
  • View the Kubernetes resources that belong to an application and the events reported for them.

All application deployments and synchronizations are performed through ArgoCD. Avoid making persistent manual changes to resources managed by ArgoCD, because a later synchronization can overwrite them.

items.title: Troubleshoot a deployment
items.text:
Start with ArgoCD when an application does not deploy or synchronize:

  1. Open the affected application.
  2. Check its synchronization and health status.
  3. Open failed or unhealthy resources.
  4. Review the synchronization result, resource events, and reported errors.

Then inspect the corresponding resources directly on the cluster:

kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
kubectl describe <resource-type> <resource-name> --namespace <namespace>
kubectl logs <pod-name> --namespace <namespace>

For remote managed clusters, run these commands from the cluster toolbox on the management cluster.

For multi-container pods, add --container <container-name> to the logs command. The resource status, events, and container logs usually show whether the problem is in Argo CD synchronization or in the deployed workload itself.

items.title: Add an availability zone
items.text:
The console lists an availability zone only after the management API knows which controller to call. That registration is separate from installing the AZ stack, and it is the same whether the AZ runs on the management cluster or somewhere else.

Install the management plane and the AZ first. Then connect them with the settings below.

items.title: AZ on the management cluster
items.text:
A hyperconverged AZ on the management cluster is already registered. The system chart defines it under the code local, with destination in-cluster. Install that AZ as clusters.local. Do not add a second code for the same cluster.

See The default local AZ. Set local to null there when the management cluster should not host an AZ.

items.title: Add any other AZ
items.text: Pick a code, for example paris-1. Use that same code as the key under clusters when you install the AZ.

items.title: 1. Controller
items.text:
On the AZ cluster, set the controller name and the secret the API will send. The secret must match the API entry in the next step.

When the API is not running on this cluster, expose the controller so the management cluster can reach it:

clusters:
  paris-1:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        superphenix-controller:
          values:
            config:
              azName: "Paris 1"
              http:
                authSecret: "replace-with-a-shared-secret"
            ingress:
              enabled: true
              hosts:
                - host: controller.paris-1.example
                  paths:
                    - path: /

Apply this with the same Helm upgrade you use to install the AZ. The controller chart leaves ingress disabled; the in-cluster Service is enough only when the API runs in this cluster.

items.title: 2. API
items.text:
On the management cluster, add the AZ to the API configuration and upgrade the operator release.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            azs:
              paris-1:
                name: "Paris 1"
                # URL the API can call. Use the controller Service URL when both
                # run in one cluster; otherwise use the ingress hostname.
                controllerUrl: "https://controller.paris-1.example"
                authSecret: "replace-with-a-shared-secret"
                # Cluster name, from `.clusters` in the superphenix-operator chart.
                destination: "paris-1"
            productsConfig:
              argoApp:
                kubernetes:
                  azDomains:
                    paris-1:
                      # Host the in-cluster API proxy uses to reach control planes.
                      internal: console.example.org
                      # "%s" is replaced by the Kubernetes cluster ID.
                      external: "%s.console.example.org"
Field Role name Name shown in the console. controllerUrl Base URL of that AZ's Superphenix controller. authSecret Shared with apps.superphenix-controller.values.config.http.authSecret on that AZ. destination Argo CD cluster that receives this AZ's applications. logoUrl Optional logo for the console. whitelist Optional list of organization IDs allowed to see this AZ. Empty means every organization. Private availability zones details how to add whitelisted organizations. azDomains.<code>.internal Host used inside the cluster to reach Kubernetes control planes for this AZ. azDomains.<code>.external Public control-plane hostname template. %s is the cluster ID.

Upgrade the operator release as described in Applying configuration changes.

The AZ appears in the console once the API can reach the controller. Open it from Accessing Superphenix.

items.title: Applying configuration changes
items.text: Changes to the management plane and to an availability zone are values on the superphenix-operator release. The operator writes those values onto a Cluster resource, and Argo CD syncs the applications on that cluster.

items.title: Management plane
items.text:
Management applications (the console, the API, Kratos, Permify, and PostgreSQL) are set under management.systemConfiguration. That object is copied onto the management Cluster.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            userSettings:
              userIsActiveOnCreate: true

The pages under Configuring the management components detail all the settings available in here.

Argo CD itself is installed by the operator chart, so its settings live beside management, under config.argocd.values.

items.title: Availability zone
items.text:
Applications that run on an availability zone are set under clusters.<code>.systemConfiguration. The key is the AZ code: local when the zone runs on the management cluster, and the code you chose in Add an availability zone otherwise.

clusters:
  paris-1:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        rook-local-cluster:
          values:
            ingress:
              dashboard:
                host:
                  name: ceph.admin.example.org

items.title: Upgrade the release
items.text:
Add the keys to the values file you already pass for this release, then upgrade:

OPERATOR_VERSION="$(curl -fsSL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/super-phenix/superphenix/releases/latest | sed 's#.*/v##')"

helm upgrade superphenix-operator \
  "oci://ghcr.io/super-phenix/charts/superphenix-operator:${OPERATOR_VERSION}" \
  --namespace superphenix-system \
  -f values.yaml

Replace OPERATOR_VERSION by your vesion of Superphenix or use the latest to upgrade your version.

Helm merges that file with the chart defaults. A later upgrade still needs the same -f file, or the keys you added are dropped.

Wait until the application you changed is Synced and Healthy in Argo CD before you test. Accessing Superphenix covers opening Argo CD.

items.title: NAT gateway traffic to its host node
items.text:
Traffic leaving a NAT gateway is blackholed when its destination is an address on the physical node that hosts the gateway. This behavior is caused by a macvlan limitation: a macvlan interface cannot communicate directly with its host.

As a result, a VM that uses the NAT gateway might be unable to reach a node address. This can affect the Getting started deployment when the console DNS record points directly to a node. It is especially problematic for Kubernetes as a Service clusters that need to reach the Superphenix control plane.

Use a load balancer in front of the nodes and point the DNS record to the load balancer. The load balancer forwards traffic to a node without relying on direct communication between the NAT gateway and its host.

As a temporary workaround, schedule the NAT gateway on a node other than the destination node. This is less reliable because rescheduling the gateway onto the destination node causes the limitation to recur.

items.title: Automated tuning
items.text:
Superphenix ships a TuneD-based daemon that applies performance-oriented settings at runtime. Enable it from the system configuration:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    tuned:
      enabled: true

A privileged DaemonSet runs on every node (including control-plane nodes). At startup, each pod reads a per-node label to choose the active profile, runs tuned, and reloads if the default profile changes. If the node has no label, it uses the default profile which optimizes for throughput, compute latency, and network latency.

items.title: Per-node profile selection
items.text:
Assign a profile with the node label (default key: performance.superphenix.net/profile):

kubectl label node <node-name> performance.superphenix.net/profile=latency-performance

Remove the label to revert to the default:

kubectl label node <node-name> performance.superphenix.net/profile-

The label value must match a profile name defined in chart values (or already present on the node image).

Restart required after label changes

Updating the profile label on a node does not cause the running tuned pod to pick up the new value. Restart the tuned DaemonSet pod on that node manually so it reads the label again at startup.

items.title: Custom profiles
items.text:
Declare additional or replacement profiles under the profiles key in the tuned chart values. Each key is a profile name; the value is the raw tuned.conf content:

profiles:
  my-custom-profile: |
    [main]
    summary=My custom tuning profile

    [cpu]
    governor=performance

    [sysctl]
    vm.swappiness=10

Profile names must be unique, start with a letter or number, and may contain letters, numbers, hyphens, dots, and underscores. Use custom profiles when you need workload-specific sysctl, CPU, or network tuning beyond the defaults.

Boot-time kernel parameters, such as C-state limits, are set with Manual tuning.

items.title: Manual tuning
items.text:
Optimizations at this layer are configured where Talos Linux runs your nodes. The Talos guide Performance tuning is a good starting point for CPU scaling governors, processor sleep states, and related kernel command-line parameters.

Typical changes include cpufreq.default_governor=performance and limits on C-states (for example intel_idle.max_cstate=0 on Intel, or amd_pstate=active on AMD). See the Talos guide for your hardware.

Reboot required

Kernel parameters applied through Talos machine configuration (for example .machine.install.extraKernelArgs) take effect after a node reboot or a no-op upgrade to the same Talos version. Plan a maintenance window when tuning production nodes this way.

These settings are static. To change profiles at runtime, use Automated tuning.

items.title: Accepting new users automatically
items.text:
With automatic acceptance, a person who can open the registration page receives an active account and can sign in immediately. To hold accounts until an administrator approves them, use Validating users manually.

The login page and the public registration warning are in Accessing Superphenix.

items.title: Leave new accounts active
items.text:
userIsActiveOnCreate is true in the system chart by default.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            userSettings:
              userIsActiveOnCreate: true

The flag applies to accounts created after the API reloads it. Accounts that are already inactive stay inactive until you set is_active in the database, as described in Validating users manually.

items.title: What registration creates
items.text:
On the first successful sign-in, the API stores the Kratos identity and creates:

  • A user row with is_active set from userIsActiveOnCreate.
  • A personal organization named Personal Org, owned by that user.
  • A project named default in that organization.

When default project resources are enabled, that project also receives a default VPC and subnet in each availability zone the organization can see.

Anyone who can reach https://<console-domain>/auth/registration can complete this flow. On a console that is reachable from the internet, restrict the network or switch to manual validation.

items.title: Custom CSS
items.text: The console theme is a stylesheet of CSS custom properties. Set themeOverride to replace the built-in override file. The variables you can set, and their defaults, are in the console theme override template. Theming describes how those variables apply to the console.

items.title: Set the override
items.text:
Add the stylesheet and upgrade the release.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-console:
        values:
          config:
            themeOverride: |
              html {
                --primary-50: #1e88e5;
              }

Tokens are declared on html. Set only the ones you want to change.

The console tells browsers to cache CSS for one year. After a sync, reload the page so the browser fetches theme-override.css again.

items.title: Auto-creating resources for users on project creation
items.text:
When default resources are enabled, creating a project also creates a VPC and a subnet in every availability zone that organization can see. The default project created for a new account at first sign-in goes through the same path. Turn the flag off when tenants should start from an empty project.

The objects are the console VPC and Subnet. What those objects do is described in VPC and Subnet.
path: Auto-creating resources for users on project creation

items.title: Enable or disable
items.text:
The system chart sets enableProjectDefaultResources to true. Add the override and upgrade the release:

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            userSettings:
              enableProjectDefaultResources: false

The flag is read when a project is created. Projects that already have a default VPC and subnet keep them. Projects created while the flag is off stay empty.
path: Auto-creating resources for users on project creation

items.title: What gets created
items.text:
For each availability zone returned for that organization, the API creates:

Object Name Source VPC default productsConfig.defaultVpc.productName Subnet default productsConfig.defaultSubnet.productName

The subnet is created inside that VPC.

The API defaults for the subnet, used when the system chart does not override them:

Field Default Effect protocol Dual IPv4 and IPv6 ipv4 10.10.0.0/16 IPv4 CIDR ipv6 fd00:10:10::/64 IPv6 CIDR natGatewayEnabled false No NAT gateway on the default subnet private false The subnet stays reachable from other subnets in the VPC. true isolates it. See Subnet. dnsV4 1.1.1.1 IPv4 resolver dnsV6 2606:4700:4700::1111 IPv6 resolver

Override any of these under config.productsConfig in the same API values. Later projects use the new template. Existing default subnets are left as they were created.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            productsConfig:
              defaultVpc:
                productName: default
              defaultSubnet:
                productName: default
                protocol: Dual
                ipv4: 10.20.0.0/16
                ipv6: fd00:10:20::/64
                natGatewayEnabled: false
                private: false
                dnsV4: 1.1.1.1
                dnsV6: 2606:4700:4700::1111

Two projects in the same availability zone each receive their own default VPC and subnet. The names match. The underlying networks are separate.
path: Auto-creating resources for users on project creation

items.title: Hardening of exposed HTTP dashboards
items.text:
The Ceph dashboard and Argo CD are published through Ingress on the cluster that runs them. Both authenticate their own users. Both become reachable by anyone who can open the hostname, as soon as DNS points that name at the cluster. Keep those hostnames on a network that only platform administrators can reach, and change the generated passwords after the first login.

Day-to-day sign-in for Argo CD is in Accessing Superphenix. Argo CD will recreate an Ingress you delete by hand. Change the values below and upgrade the release so the sync keeps the hardened settings.

items.title: Ceph dashboard
items.text:
On a hyperconverged cluster and on a decoupled storage cluster, the system chart enables the Rook dashboard and an Ingress for it.

Sign in as admin. Rook stores the generated password in the rook-ceph-dashboard-password Secret in spx-storage:

kubectl --namespace spx-storage get secret rook-ceph-dashboard-password \
  --output jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
echo

Change that password in the dashboard after the first login. Rook documents the user and the Secret in the Ceph dashboard guide.

items.title: Choose a hostname
items.text:
Set host.name to a name you control, on the cluster that runs Ceph. The key under clusters is the AZ code.

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        rook-local-cluster:
          values:
            ingress:
              dashboard:
                host:
                  name: ceph.admin.example.org
                  path: /
                tls:
                  - hosts:
                      - ceph.admin.example.org
                    secretName: ceph-dashboard-tls

Publish ceph.admin.example.org only where administrators sit. The chart default ceph.example.org is a placeholder. If that name, or your replacement, resolves to a node and cert-manager can complete the HTTP challenge, the dashboard is on the internet with the admin password as the gate.

The Ingress is rendered whenever ingress.dashboard.host is set, and the system chart sets it. Leaving the placeholder in place keeps an Ingress object for ceph.example.org.

items.title: Disable the Ingress
items.text:
Set host to null on the cluster that runs Ceph. Helm drops a null key, so the chart default hostname is removed and Rook does not render the Ingress.

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        rook-local-cluster:
          values:
            ingress:
              dashboard:
                host: null

The key under clusters is the AZ code. The dashboard Service rook-ceph-mgr-dashboard stays in spx-storage, so the dashboard is still reachable from inside that cluster.

items.title: Argo CD
items.text: The operator installs Argo CD with an Ingress enabled, server.insecure: true, and TLS terminated on the Ingress. The hostname you set at install time is config.argocd.values.server.ingress.hostname, described in Configuring the management stack. The initial admin password and the sign-in URL are in Accessing Superphenix. Change the password after the first login.

items.title: Remove the public Ingress
items.text:
config:
  argocd:
    values:
      server:
        ingress:
          enabled: false

User values are merged on top of the operator's Argo CD defaults, so enabled: false overrides the built-in Ingress. Reach the API with kubectl from the cluster toolbox instead.

items.title: Turn off the UI shell and status badges
items.text:
Keep the Ingress, and still remove the two features that go beyond reading application status:

config:
  argocd:
    values:
      configs:
        cm:
          exec.enabled: false
          statusbadge.enabled: false

With exec.enabled false, the UI no longer offers a pod shell. Administrators still have the cluster toolbox for kubectl and k9s.

items.title: MFA and recovery
items.text:
Account recovery is enabled in the management chart. TOTP and backup codes stay off until you enable them in Second factors. Recovery codes and one-time login codes are delivered by the Kratos courier, so set Sending emails first.

The console serves the Kratos flows at these paths:

Flow URL Login https://<console-domain>/auth/login Registration https://<console-domain>/auth/registration Recovery https://<console-domain>/auth/recovery Settings https://<console-domain>/auth/settings

Email verification is disabled by default (selfservice.flows.verification.enabled: false). Recovery does not wait for a verified address.

items.title: Password recovery
items.text:
The login page links Forgot password to /auth/recovery. The user enters the account email. Kratos emails a code and the console asks for that code. The code method lifespan is 15 minutes by default.

After a successful recovery, Kratos runs the revoke_active_sessions hook, so other sessions for that identity are signed out.

A password change from /auth/settings asks the user to sign in again when the session is older than 15 minutes (privileged_session_max_age).

To stop self-service recovery, set the flow off and upgrade the release. The login page then reports that recovery is disabled.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      kratos:
        values:
          kratos:
            config:
              selfservice:
                flows:
                  recovery:
                    enabled: false

items.title: One-time login codes
items.text: selfservice.methods.code is enabled with a 15-minute lifespan. The login page shows a code step when Kratos offers that method. The code is emailed through the same courier as recovery. That code signs the user in on its own. A second factor is the TOTP method below.

items.title: Second factors
items.text:
TOTP, backup codes, and WebAuthn are off by default.

You can enable with the following configuration. Field names are the Kratos self-hosted MFA configuration.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      kratos:
        values:
          kratos:
            config:
              selfservice:
                methods:
                  totp:
                    enabled: true
                    config:
                      issuer: Superphenix
                  lookup_secret:
                    enabled: true
                  webauthn:
                    enabled: true
                    config:
                      passwordless: false
                      rp:
                        display_name: Superphenix
                        # Parent domain of the console host.
                        id: example.org
                        # Scheme and host of the page that starts the WebAuthn prompt.
                        origin: https://console.example.org

issuer is the name shown in the authenticator app. TOTP and WebAuthn describe the credentials. origin has to match the scheme and host of that page. The chart's registration flow already includes a webauthn hook that shows the verification UI. The method stays disabled until this block sets enabled: true.

The shipped identity schema marks email as the password identifier and as the recovery address. It has no credentials.totp.account_name, so the authenticator app has no account label from that schema.

items.title: Private availability zones
items.text:
A private availability zone is visible only to the organizations listed on its whitelist. Every other organization is treated as if the zone does not exist: it is omitted from their zone list, and API calls that name it return not found. An empty whitelist, which is the default, leaves the zone visible to every organization.

Register the zone first. Add an availability zone covers the controller URL, shared secret, destination, and azDomains entry. This page only adds the whitelist.

items.title: Find the organization id
items.text:
Organization ids are the id column of organizations. Open the API database, then:

Info

We are working on scripts in the cluster toolbox for these queries.

SELECT id, name
FROM organizations
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
ORDER BY name;

Copy the id values of the organizations that should see the zone.

items.title: Set the whitelist
items.text:
Add whitelist on the zone entry and upgrade the release. The example below is the paris-1 zone from Add an availability zone. Repeat the keys that zone already has so the upgrade keeps them, and add whitelist.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            azs:
              paris-1:
                name: "Paris 1"
                controllerUrl: "https://controller.paris-1.example"
                authSecret: "replace-with-a-shared-secret"
                destination: "paris-1"
                whitelist:
                  - "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"

To make a zone public again, set whitelist to [].

items.title: What members and non-members see
items.text:
An organization on the list sees the zone in the console and can create resources there. An organization that is absent does not see it.

Put every organization that must keep using the zone on the list before you apply it. A zone that already holds a project's resources disappears from that project's console when its organization is left off the whitelist. The resources remain in the zone.

items.title: Sending emails
items.text:
Kratos sends password-recovery codes and one-time login codes through its courier. This page sets the SMTP server those messages use. Account recovery itself is covered in MFA and recovery.

The management chart always sets a courier block. The default connection is a placeholder, smtps://dummy@example.org:password@localhost:465/, so a fresh install does not deliver mail. Replace it before anyone depends on recovery or a login code.

items.title: Set the SMTP server
items.text:
Add the courier settings to the operator values and upgrade the release. The kratos application must be Synced and Healthy before you send a test message.

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      kratos:
        values:
          kratos:
            config:
              courier:
                smtp:
                  connection_uri: smtps://mailer:replace-with-a-password@smtp.example.org:465/
                  from_address: no-reply@example.org
                  from_name: Superphenix
Field Role connection_uri SMTP server. smtps:// opens TLS on connect. The chart default uses port 465. from_address Address recipients see as the sender. from_name Display name on the message. The chart default is Superphenix Console.

Percent-encode reserved characters in the username and password. A password that contains @, :, or / will otherwise be parsed as part of the URI.

Kratos stores the identity and the recovery code in the kratos database. The message itself leaves the cluster only through this URI. A firewall that blocks the management pods from the mail server leaves the code in Kratos and the user with an empty inbox.

items.title: Confirm delivery
items.text:
Open the console login page and choose Forgot password, or start a recovery from https://<console-domain>/auth/recovery. Kratos responds that a code was sent when the address matches an account. The message arrives only when the courier can open connection_uri.

If nothing arrives, read the kratos pod logs for the courier error, then check that the management cluster can reach the SMTP host and port. The placeholder host localhost fails this check on purpose.

items.title: Setting super-admins
items.text:
A super-admin is a user id on the API's superAdmins list. Permission checks on the API succeed for those ids, and the console is told that the user holds every permission it asked about. The list is empty by default, so nobody has that bypass until you add an id.

The id is the id column of the users table. Copy it from the database as described below. Open the API database first.

items.title: Choose the user
items.text:
The account must already exist and be active. A user row is created at the first sign-in.

Info

We are working on scripts in the cluster toolbox for these queries.

SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE email = 'admin@example.org'
  AND deleted_at IS NULL;

items.title: Add the id
items.text:
Set the list and upgrade the release:

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            superAdmins:
              - "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"

Replace the example with the id from the query. Add one list entry per user. An empty list, or removing the key so the chart default [] applies again, turns the bypass off after the API reloads.

items.title: What the bypass allows
items.text:
For a signed-in user whose id is on the list:

  • Organization, project, quota, audit, and product permission checks succeed.
  • The permission list returned to the console is the full set for the object they opened, so the console shows every action.
  • An organization response includes every project in that organization.
  • A project summary includes every product type.

While the list is non-empty, the API also mounts these routes. A caller who is not on the list receives 404.

Method and path Returns GET /api/v1/project-manager/users Every user GET /api/v1/project-manager/organizations Every organization GET /api/v1/project-manager/projects Every project GET /api/v1/project-manager/products Every product

Send the user's access token in Authorization: Bearer. The routes are not registered at all when superAdmins is empty.

Platform-wide access

A super-admin passes permission checks in every organization and project the API evaluates. Keep the list to operators who already administer the management cluster, and remove an id when that person should return to ordinary membership.

items.title: Validating users manually
items.text: Manual validation lets people register, then keeps the account out of the console until an administrator marks it active. The system default leaves userIsActiveOnCreate at true, so a registration can sign in immediately until you change it here.

items.title: Hold new accounts inactive
items.text:
Set userIsActiveOnCreate to false and upgrade the release:

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-api:
        values:
          config:
            userSettings:
              userIsActiveOnCreate: false

Registrations that complete after the API reloads this value are stored with is_active false. The API still creates the personal organization Personal Org and the project default at first sign-in. The console session is refused until the row is active.

The user can authenticate with Kratos and then lands on Inactive Account. That page says the account cannot open the console and offers the address in config.supportEmail. The console chart default for that address is support@example.org. Set a mailbox you read:

management:
  systemConfiguration:
    apps:
      superphenix-console:
        values:
          config:
            supportEmail: platform@example.org

environment.js is served with Cache-Control: no-cache, so a reload shows the new address.

Existing active users stay active. The flag is written only when the user row is created.

items.title: Open the API database
items.text:
User and organization rows live in the superphenix database on the management PostgreSQL instance. The pod has the password in POSTGRES_PASSWORD.

kubectl --namespace superphenix-system exec --stdin --tty \
  statefulset/postgres --container postgres -- \
  bash -c 'PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" psql --username "$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname "$POSTGRES_DB"'

items.title: Activate an account
items.text:
Info

We are working on scripts in the cluster toolbox for these queries.

List accounts that are waiting:

SELECT id, email, is_active, created_at
FROM users
WHERE is_active = false
  AND deleted_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at;

Activate the one you have checked:

UPDATE users
SET is_active = true
WHERE email = 'user@example.org'
  AND deleted_at IS NULL;

Ask the user to sign in again. The next session request reads is_active and issues console tokens.

To close an account later, set is_active back to false. An access token that was already issued stays valid until it expires. The API default for that lifetime is 1 hour. A refresh after that is refused, and API tokens for the user are refused as soon as the row is inactive.

items.title: Configure NAT gateways
items.text:
NAT gateways connect private Superphenix subnets to an external network. Before creating NAT gateways or Elastic IPs (EIPs), configure:

  1. An external interface with the same name on every Talos node.
  2. An external subnet from which Superphenix can allocate NAT gateway addresses.
  3. The EIP allocation subnet and, when required, the BGP speaker settings for each availability zone (AZ).

items.title: Configure the external interface in Talos
items.text:
Every node must expose the external network through an interface with the same name. This example uses ext0:

machine:
  network:
    interfaces:
      - interface: ext0
        routes:
          - network: 0.0.0.0/0
            gateway: 10.81.5.1

Replace the addressing and gateway with values for your external network. The interface can be a physical NIC, bond, or VLAN, but its Talos name must be identical on every node.

If physical interface names differ between nodes, add a LinkAliasConfig to each node's Talos configuration. Keep name identical and change the MAC address for each node:

---
apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: LinkAliasConfig
name: ext0
selector:
  match: mac(link.permanent_addr) == "00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e"

Do not use kernel-style names such as eth0, ens3, or enp0s31f6 as the common alias.

items.title: Configure the external subnet
items.text:
Define the external subnet and its network attachment in the AZ's system configuration. The network attachment must use the common Talos interface as its master:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    misc:
      values:
        objects:
          external-subnet:
            spec:
              protocol: IPv4
              cidrBlock: 10.81.5.0/24
              gateway: 10.81.5.1
              excludeIps:
                - 10.81.5.0..10.81.5.31
                - 10.81.5.255
          external-subnet-nad:
            spec:
              config: '{
                  "cniVersion": "0.3.0",
                  "type": "macvlan",
                  "master": "ext0",
                  "mode": "bridge",
                  "ipam": {
                    "type": "kube-ovn",
                    "server_socket": "/run/openvswitch/kube-ovn-daemon.sock",
                    "provider": "external-subnet.kube-system"
                  }
                }'

Exclude the network and broadcast addresses, node addresses, router addresses, and any other addresses that Superphenix must not allocate. In a BGP deployment, this subnet is only used to address the NAT gateways and their BGP speakers. A private RFC 1918 range is recommended because these addresses do not need to be public.

External network connectivity

The common interface on every node must reach the external subnet. The backbone must then learn how to reach the EIPs through either ARP or BGP.

items.title: Choose how to announce EIPs
items.text: Superphenix can announce EIPs to the backbone using either ARP or BGP.

items.title: ARP announcement
items.text:
ARP is the default and requires no BGP configuration. Superphenix answers ARP requests for an EIP on the external network, allowing the upstream gateway to send traffic directly to the NAT gateway.

With ARP, EIPs must belong to the external Layer 2 subnet so that the upstream gateway can resolve them.

ARP is appropriate when:

  • The NAT gateways and upstream gateway share the same Layer 2 network.
  • You want the simplest setup with no BGP peering.
  • The external broadcast domain is small enough to extend to every relevant node.

Its main limitation is that EIP reachability depends on a shared Layer 2 domain. Extending that domain across racks or network zones can increase the broadcast scope and make the network harder to scale.

items.title: BGP announcement
items.text:
BGP advertises EIP routes to one or more upstream routers. It requires an ASN, a remote ASN, and at least one reachable neighbor.

Unlike ARP, BGP does not require EIPs to belong to external-subnet. The external subnet provides private addresses for the NAT gateways and connectivity to their BGP neighbors, while EIPs can be allocated from a separate public prefix and advertised to the backbone.

BGP is preferable when:

  • The backbone is routed and does not extend the external Layer 2 domain.
  • EIP routes must be propagated beyond one subnet or network segment.
  • You want explicit routing policy and better route visibility on the backbone.
  • You need routing features such as multiple peers or graceful restart.

BGP requires coordination with the network team and matching peer configuration on the upstream routers, but it generally scales better across racks, network zones, and AZs.

Recommended BGP addressing

Use a private subnet, such as 10.81.5.0/24, for NAT gateway and BGP speaker addresses. Use a separate public prefix for EIPs. The examples use 192.0.2.0/24, which is reserved by RFC 5737 for documentation; replace it with a public prefix routed to your organization.

Create a separate EIP subnet for BGP

Create the public EIP subnet in the same way as external-subnet. Unlike the existing external-subnet objects, these are new resources, so include their apiVersion, kind, and metadata.

A network attachment definition (NAD) is still required, even though BGP-routed EIPs are not mounted on a host interface. Its macvlan master can therefore use a placeholder such as fake:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    misc:
      values:
        objects:
          192.0.2.0-24:
            apiVersion: kubeovn.io/v1
            kind: Subnet
            metadata:
              name: 192.0.2.0-24
            spec:
              protocol: IPv4
              cidrBlock: 192.0.2.0/24
              gateway: 192.0.2.1
              excludeIps:
                - 192.0.2.0..192.0.2.1
                - 192.0.2.255
          192.0.2.0-24-nad:
            apiVersion: "k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1"
            kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
            metadata:
              name: 192.0.2.0-24
              namespace: kube-system
            spec:
              config: '{
                  "cniVersion": "0.3.0",
                  "type": "macvlan",
                  "master": "fake",
                  "mode": "bridge",
                  "ipam": {
                    "type": "kube-ovn",
                    "server_socket": "/run/openvswitch/kube-ovn-daemon.sock",
                    "provider": "192.0.2.0-24.kube-system"
                  }
                }'

The placeholder interface is never used to carry EIP traffic. The BGP speaker advertises the EIPs, and the backbone routes their traffic to the NAT gateway through external-subnet.

items.title: Configure NAT gateway defaults
items.text:
Pass the EIP and NAT gateway defaults through the AZ's systemConfiguration, under apps.superphenix-controller.values.config.productsConfig. To use ARP announcements, set eipDefault.externalSubnet to external-subnet and omit bgpSpeaker, or leave it disabled.

For BGP, set config.productsConfig.eipDefault.externalSubnet to the separate IPAM subnet that contains the public EIP pool. This adjusts the controller so that it allocates EIPs from the public prefix instead of the private subnet used by the NAT gateways.

The following example assumes:

  • external-subnet is 10.81.5.0/24 and provides private addresses to the NAT gateways.
  • The upstream BGP router is 10.81.5.1.
  • The EIP subnet created above is named 192.0.2.0-24 and represents the example public prefix 192.0.2.0/24.
systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    superphenix-controller:
      values:
        config:
          productsConfig:
            eipDefault:
              externalSubnet: "192.0.2.0-24"
            natGatewayDefault:
              bgpSpeaker:
                enabled: true
                asn: 64892
                remoteAsn: 64890
                neighbors:
                  - 10.81.5.1
                enableGracefulRestart: true
                extraArgs:
                  - "-v5"
                  - "--graceful-restart"

Apply this configuration to each AZ that should advertise EIP routes. Values can differ by AZ to match the local routers and autonomous systems.

The BGP speaker accepts these settings under config.productsConfig.natGatewayDefault.bgpSpeaker:

  • enabled: enables or disables BGP route advertisement.
  • asn: the local ASN used by the AZ's NAT gateways.
  • remoteAsn: the ASN expected from the upstream BGP peers.
  • neighbors: one or more upstream BGP peer addresses.
  • holdTime: the BGP hold time, expressed as a duration such as "90s".
  • routerId: the BGP router ID.
  • password: the BGP session password. Store sensitive values through your normal secret-management process.
  • enableGracefulRestart: enables BGP graceful restart.
  • extraArgs: additional arguments passed to the BGP speaker.

Only enabled and the settings required by your network need to be specified. Coordinate the ASNs, neighbor addresses, authentication, timers, and graceful-restart behavior with the upstream router configuration.

items.title: Hairpin NAT
items.text:
Hairpin NAT lets a workload reach another workload through its Elastic IP (EIP), even when both workloads are on the private network. This is also known as NAT loopback.

Without hairpin NAT, traffic sent to the EIP may leave the private network or fail to return through the same NAT gateway. Applications then need different internal and external addresses for the same service.

Superphenix supports hairpin NAT. When a private client connects to an EIP, the NAT gateway:

  1. Replaces the destination EIP with the private IP of the target workload (DNAT).
  2. Replaces the client's private source IP with that same EIP (SNAT).

The source translation forces the response back through the NAT gateway, which reverses both translations and returns the response to the client.

In this example:

  • The client at 10.20.0.2 connects to the service EIP 198.51.100.20.
  • The NAT gateway changes the destination to the server's private IP, 10.20.0.3.
  • The NAT gateway also changes the source from 10.20.0.2 to 198.51.100.20.
  • The server therefore sees a connection from 198.51.100.20, not from the client's private IP.
  • The client continues to see 198.51.100.20 as the service address.

Preserving the client address

Because hairpin NAT translates the source address, the target workload cannot use the packet's source IP to identify the original client. If the application needs that identity, pass it at the application layer or use the private service address directly.

Hairpin NAT applies to both one-to-one EIP mappings and ports exposed with DNAT rules. The EIP and its destination must already be configured on the subnet's NAT gateway.

items.title: IPv6 configuration
items.text:
Superphenix supports both IPv4 and IPv6, and some of the largest Superphenix deployments are IPv6-first.

Superphenix is usually deployed in dual-stack mode with IPv6 as the preferred address family. IPv6 is used for internal communication, while IPv4 preserves connectivity to external components and services that are not available over IPv6, such as GitHub.

The first address family in the configuration is the preferred family. Superphenix uses it for internal communication across both physical and virtual networks.

Keep the address-family order consistent

Use the same IPv4/IPv6 order for the Talos pod and service subnets, the kubelet node IP ranges, the etcd advertised subnets, and the Kube-OVN network configuration. Kube-OVN master addresses must use the address family listed first.

items.title: Running dual stack with IPv4 first
items.text:
The configuration from Getting started places IPv4 before IPv6. Configure the Talos pod and service subnets, etcd advertised subnets, and kubelet node IP ranges in that order:

cluster:
  network:
    podSubnets:
      - 10.0.0.0/12
      - fd00:100:0000:0::/96
    serviceSubnets:
      - 10.16.0.0/12
      - fd00:100:ffff:0::/112
  etcd:
    advertisedSubnets:
      - 192.168.1.0/24
      - fd00:1::/64

machine:
  kubelet:
    nodeIP:
      validSubnets:
        - 192.168.1.0/24
        - fd00:1::/64

The kubelet and etcd ranges select node addresses, so replace the example ranges with the IPv4 and IPv6 ranges of your node network.

Configure Kube-OVN with IPv4 first as well. Because IPv4 is preferred, masterNodes must contain the IPv4 addresses of the control-plane nodes:

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        kubeovn:
          values:
            masterNodes: "192.168.1.150,192.168.1.151,192.168.1.153"
            networking:
              pods:
                cidr:
                  v4: "10.0.0.0/12"
                  v6: "fd00:100:0000:0::/96"
                gateways:
                  v4: "10.0.0.1"
                  v6: "fd00:100:0000:0::1"
              services:
                cidr:
                  v4: "10.16.0.0/12"
                  v6: "fd00:100:ffff:0::/112"
              join:
                cidr:
                  v4: "100.64.0.0/12"
                  v6: "fd00:100:64::/112"

With this configuration, Superphenix prioritizes IPv4 for communication within the physical node network and virtual workload networks.

items.title: Running dual stack with IPv6 first
items.text:
To prefer IPv6, reverse the address-family order everywhere. In the Talos configuration, list IPv6 before IPv4 for the pod and service subnets, etcd advertised subnets, and kubelet node IP ranges:

cluster:
  network:
    podSubnets:
      - fd00:100:0000:0::/96
      - 10.0.0.0/12
    serviceSubnets:
      - fd00:100:ffff:0::/112
      - 10.16.0.0/12
  etcd:
    advertisedSubnets:
      - fd00:1::/64
      - 192.168.1.0/24

machine:
  kubelet:
    nodeIP:
      validSubnets:
        - fd00:1::/64
        - 192.168.1.0/24

Configure the Kube-OVN ranges in the same IPv6-first order. Because IPv6 is preferred, masterNodes must contain the IPv6 addresses of the control-plane nodes:

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        kubeovn:
          values:
            masterNodes: "fd00:1::150,fd00:1::151,fd00:1::153"
            networking:
              pods:
                cidr:
                  v6: "fd00:100:0000:0::/96"
                  v4: "10.0.0.0/12"
                gateways:
                  v6: "fd00:100:0000:0::1"
                  v4: "10.0.0.1"
              services:
                cidr:
                  v6: "fd00:100:ffff:0::/112"
                  v4: "10.16.0.0/12"
              join:
                cidr:
                  v6: "fd00:100:64::/112"
                  v4: "100.64.0.0/12"

With this configuration, Superphenix prioritizes IPv6 for communication within the physical node network and virtual workload networks, while IPv4 remains available for IPv4-only destinations.

items.title: Configure Ceph to use IPv6
items.text:
On the cluster that hosts Ceph, bind the Ceph public and cluster networks to IPv6 subnets through the rook-local-cluster configuration:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephClusterSpec:
          network:
            addressRanges:
              public:
                - fd00:ffff:2000::/64
              cluster:
                - fd00:ffff:2001::/96

The public subnet carries Ceph client and monitor traffic. The cluster subnet carries replication, recovery, and other traffic between Ceph daemons. Every Ceph node must have an address in the configured IPv6 subnet or subnets.

Connecting separate workload and storage clusters

For a decoupled deployment, follow Connecting a workload and storage cluster.

The bootstrapMon.ip used by the workload cluster must be an IPv6 address from the Ceph public network, and bootstrapMon.protocol must be set to IPv6. This ensures that Superphenix bootstraps the connection and retrieves the Ceph monitor list over IPv6.

bootstrapMon:
  id: a
  ip: "fd00:ffff:2000::10"
  port: "6789"
  protocol: IPv6

items.title: Setting the MTU of subnets
items.text:
The maximum transmission unit (MTU) controls the largest packet that a network interface can send without fragmentation. A consistent MTU across the complete path improves efficiency by carrying more data in each frame and reducing per-packet processing. It also allows Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) to select a packet size that every hop can forward.

An incorrect MTU can cause fragmentation, reduce performance, or create a PMTU black hole when the ICMP messages required by PMTUD are filtered.

Recommended platform MTU: 9000

Configure an MTU of 9000 end to end on the platform links and network fabric. Jumbo frames improve throughput and reduce CPU overhead, particularly for storage and east-west traffic.

items.title: Automatic MTU detection
items.text:
The Superphenix software-defined network uses GENEVE encapsulation. Superphenix reserves 100 bytes for the overlay overhead, so the MTU presented to VMs and containers is the platform MTU minus 100 bytes.

For example, a node MTU of 9000 results in an MTU of 8900 inside VMs and containers.

Automatic MTU detection is enabled by default. It currently detects the link MTU (used to egress from the node) but does not cap the detected value at 1500 for Internet-bound traffic. A maximum-MTU cap is planned for a future release. Until then, explicitly configure 1500 for Internet-facing subnets when the platform link MTU is greater than 1600. If you do not, you risk fragmentation and blackholes for traffic heading to the Internet.

items.title: Configure the MTU of user-created subnets
items.text:
It is possible to set a specific MTU for subnets created within an AZ.

If you wish to force the MTU, disable mtuAutodetection on the controller of the AZ. Then, set your desired MTU:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    superphenix-controller:
      values:
        config:
          productsConfig:
            subnets:
              mtuAutodetection: false
              mtu: 9000

Use a value supported end to end by every physical link, VLAN, bond, and switch port in the path.

Internet-facing workloads

Internet paths generally support an MTU of 1500. When the platform links use an MTU greater than 1600, pods and VMs can send packets larger than the Internet path supports after accounting for the 100-byte GENEVE overhead. This can cause fragmentation or PMTU black holes.

For subnets whose pods or VMs access the Internet, force config.productsConfig.subnets.mtu to 1500.

items.title: Adding a storage class
items.text:
Storage classes are how end users choose what type of storage they get on the platform. When someone creates a disk or bucket, they pick a class that defines what they get: media type (HDD, SSD, NVMe), QoS (IOPS, bandwidth), data protection (replication, erasure coding), and options such as encryption.

On each cluster, you define storage classes. A class appears in the console only after you map it on the AZ controller, which is covered at the end of each section below. Creating the class depends on your AZ layout:

  • Hyperconverged: storage runs on the same cluster as workloads.
  • Decoupled: the workload cluster connects to storage provided by a dedicated storage cluster.

In both cases, every storage class is backed by a storage pool. The pool defines the physical media and data protection; one pool can serve several classes with different QoS or encryption settings. For example, an NVMe pool with 3-way replication could back two classes. One could be capped at 100 MB/s and another be configured with encryption, while the data lands on the same underlying pool.

You'll need a storage pool to proceed. The sections below expose those pools through storage classes, whether for block storage, filesystem or object storage purposes.

items.title: Adding a block storage class
items.text:
This section covers adding a storage class for block storage. They're used by end users pick when they create disks and other block volumes (such as PVCs in Kubernetes clusters deployed within Superphenix).

A block storage class is the user-facing catalog entry for block storage. It points at a pool and adds policies such as QoS and encryption so tenants can pick the right offering when they create disks.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • At least one storage pool already exists on the cluster that hosts the storage. See Adding a storage pool.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Add the block storage class under systemConfiguration on the Cluster resource (or via the superphenix-operator Helm chart), using the rook-connection chart. Choose the example that matches your AZ layout.

Where to apply this configuration

Configure the storage class on the cluster that consumes the storage:

  • Hyperconverged: the same cluster that hosts the pool.
  • Decoupled: the workload cluster. Remote connection fields point at the storage cluster.
HyperconvergedDecoupled

On a hyperconverged cluster, storage and workloads share the same Superphenix cluster. You only need to reference the local pool and define storage classes. No remote Ceph connection fields are necessary.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-connection:
      values:
        clusters:
          - name: "spx-storage"
            blockPools:
              # Name must match an existing storage pool. If you're creating a storage class for an erasure
              # coded pool, you need to specify the name of the metadata pool here. If you followed the previous
              # steps to add an EC pool, the name of the metadata pool will be [pool name]-metadata.
              - name: "[pool-name]"
                storageClasses:
                  - name: "[storage-class-name]"
                    # StorageClass name will be "<cluster>.<name>" unless fullName is set.
                    # Name must be unique across every storage class in the cluster.
                    # fullName: ""
                    # Data pool for erasure-coded storage classes (leave empty for replicated).
                    # If you followed the previous steps to add an EC pool, the name of the data pool will be
                    # the name of your pool.
                    dataPool: ""
                    # If set to true, this storage class will be used as the default when none is specified.
                    # Only one can be set per cluster. We recommend setting the pool with the less costly media (e.g. HDD).
                    default: true
                    # Enables encryption of the individual disks created from this storage class.
                    # The data will be stored within the pool encrypted.
                    encryption:
                      # Set to true to enable encryption, and provide a random passphrase.
                      enabled: false
                      # Encryption passphrase, can be a random string of characters.
                      passphrase: ""

Info

Values used to connect to a remote cluster are detailed in Connecting a workload and storage cluster.

On a decoupled AZ, create the storage class on the workload cluster and connect it to a pool on the storage cluster. That requires Ceph connection details (clusterID, credentials, bootstrap MON, and health check) plus the pool and storage class definitions.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-connection:
      values:
        clusters:
          - name: "[storage-cluster-name]" # The name of the remote storage cluster
            # Ceph cluster ID (FSID), e.g. e2a62ea1-6428-496e-a5bf-366936a8c833
            clusterID: ""
            # Pool client CephClient name, without the client. prefix
            username: "[name]"
            # Key from Secret rook-ceph-client-[name] on the storage cluster
            token: ""
            # Initial MON used to retrieve the full MON list
            bootstrapMon:
              # MON ID (must be a single letter)
              id: ""
              # IP of the MON
              ip: ""
              # Port of the MON
              port: "6789"
              # Protocol of the IP (IPv4 or IPv6)
              protocol: IPv6
            # client.csi-health, and the key from Secret rook-ceph-client-csi-health
            healthCheck:
              username: "client.csi-health"
              token: ""
            blockPools:
              # Name must match an existing storage pool. If you're creating a storage class for an erasure
              # coded pool, you need to specify the name of the metadata pool here. If you followed the previous
              # steps to add an EC pool, the name of the metadata pool will be [pool name]-metadata.
              - name: "[pool-name]" # Must match an existing pool on the storage cluster
                storageClasses:
                  - name: "[storage-class-name]"
                    # StorageClass name will be "<cluster>.<name>" unless fullName is set.
                    # Name must be unique across every storage class in the cluster.
                    # fullName: ""
                    # Data pool for erasure-coded storage classes (leave empty for replicated).
                    # If you followed the previous steps to add an EC pool, the name of the data pool will be
                    # the name of your pool.
                    dataPool: ""
                    # If set to true, this storage class will be used as the default when none is specified.
                    # Only one can be set per cluster. We recommend setting the pool with the less costly media (e.g. HDD).
                    default: true
                    # Enables encryption of the individual disks created from this storage class.
                    # The data will be stored within the pool encrypted.
                    encryption:
                      # Set to true to enable encryption, and provide a random passphrase.
                      enabled: false
                      # Encryption passphrase, can be a random string of characters.
                      passphrase: ""

For advanced storage class and connection options, see the spx-rook-connection chart values.

items.title: Expose block classes in the console
items.text:
The class above exists in Kubernetes. Console users can select it when they create a disk only after the AZ controller maps a catalog name to that StorageClass.

Set the mapping on the AZ (the cluster that runs superphenix-controller), under apps.superphenix-controller.values.config.productsConfig. The key is the name shown in the console. The value is the Kubernetes StorageClass name: <cluster>.<name>, where <cluster> is the rook-connection cluster name and <name> is the storage class name. If you set fullName, use that value instead.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    superphenix-controller:
      values:
        config:
          productsConfig:
            blockStorage:
              storageClassMapping:
                # Console name: Kubernetes StorageClass name
                block-highspeed: "[cluster].default"
                block-highspeed-encrypted: "[cluster].block-highspeed-encrypted"
                block-standard: "[cluster].block-standard"
                block-standard-encrypted: "[cluster].block-standard-encrypted"
                block-hdd: "[cluster].block-hdd"
                block-hdd-encrypted: "[cluster].block-hdd-encrypted"

A class that is missing from storageClassMapping is not offered when users create disks.

items.title: Adding an object storage class
items.text:
This section covers adding a storage class for object (S3) storage. They're used by end users when they create buckets and consume S3-compatible storage.

An object storage class is the user-facing catalog entry for S3 object storage. It exposes an object store so tenants can create and use buckets with the media, protection, and policies you define.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • At least one object store already exists on the cluster that hosts the storage. See Adding an object store.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Add the object storage class under systemConfiguration on the Cluster resource (or via the superphenix-operator Helm chart), using the rook-connection chart. Choose the example that matches your AZ layout.

Where to apply this configuration

Configure the storage class on the cluster that consumes the storage:

  • Hyperconverged: the same cluster that hosts the object store.
  • Decoupled: the workload cluster. Remote connection fields point at the storage cluster.
HyperconvergedDecoupled

On a hyperconverged cluster, storage and workloads share the same Superphenix cluster. You only need to reference the local object store and define the object storage class. No remote RGW endpoint or Ceph connection fields are necessary.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-connection:
      values:
        clusters:
          - name: "spx-storage"
            objectStores:
              - name: "[object-store-name]" # CephObjectStore name, refer to the article to create an object store
                storageClasses:
                  - name: "[storage-class-name]"
                    # StorageClass name will be "<cluster>.<name>" unless fullName is set.
                    # Name must be unique across every storage class in the cluster.
                    # fullName: ""

Info

Values used to connect to a remote cluster are detailed in Connecting a workload and storage cluster.
