On a decoupled AZ, create the object storage class on the workload cluster and connect it to an object store on the storage cluster. That requires the RGW admin keys, the remote RGW endpoints, and the object store storage class definitions.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-connection:
      values:
        clusters:
          - name: "[storage-cluster-name]" # The name of the remote storage cluster
            # Keys from Secret rook-ceph-object-user-[store]-[store] on the storage cluster
            rgwAdminOps:
              accessKey: ""
              secretKey: ""
            objectStores:
              - name: "[object-store-name]"
                # External RGW endpoints. Each entry accepts either `ip` or `hostname`.
                endpoints:
                  - ip: ""
                    # hostname: ""
                # Gateway HTTP port
                port: 80
                # Gateway HTTPS port (only set when TLS is enabled)
                securePort: 443
                # TLS configuration for the remote RGW (optional)
                # tls:
                #   enabled: false
                #   # PEM-encoded certificate the operator will trust when talking to the RGW
                #   cert: ""
                storageClasses:
                  - name: "[storage-class-name]"
                    # StorageClass name will be "<cluster>.<name>" unless fullName is set.
                    # Name must be unique across every storage class in the cluster.
                    # fullName: ""
                    reclaimPolicy: Delete

For advanced storage class and connection options, see the spx-rook-connection chart values.

items.title: Expose object classes in the console
items.text:
The class above exists in Kubernetes. Console users can select it when they create a bucket only after the AZ controller maps a catalog name to that StorageClass.

Set the mapping on the AZ, in the same controller configuration as block classes. The key is the name shown in the console. The value is the Kubernetes StorageClass name: <cluster>.<name>, or fullName when that is set.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    superphenix-controller:
      values:
        config:
          productsConfig:
            objectStorage:
              storageClassMapping:
                # Console name: Kubernetes StorageClass name
                object-silver: "[cluster].rgw-silver"

A class that is missing from storageClassMapping is not offered when users create buckets.

items.title: Adding a storage pool
items.text: A storage pool is the Ceph layer that holds the data. It chooses which disks to use and how data is protected. Storage classes then expose that pool to users with different QoS or encryption settings.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
The cluster must actually have the media and topology your pool expects:

  • An NVMe pool needs NVMe disks in the cluster (same idea for SSD or HDD).
  • 3× replication across hosts needs at least three servers that hold those disks.
  • Erasure coding (for example 4+2) typically needs at least six servers.

If the device class or failure domain does not match what is installed, the pool cannot place data safely.

items.title: Protection models
items.text:
Ceph pools use one of two data-protection models:

  • Replicated: copies of each object across failure domains. Simpler and a good fit for smaller clusters; more raw capacity for the same usable space (size 3 means 1 TB of data uses about 3 TB raw).
  • Erasure coding: data and parity chunks across failure domains. Better storage efficiency at scale; needs more hosts and has different performance trade-offs.

Prefer replication when you have few hosts or disks. Prefer erasure coding when you store large volumes of data and can spare at least six nodes.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Add the pool under systemConfiguration on the Cluster resource (or via the superphenix-operator Helm chart). Choose the example that matches your protection model.

Where to apply this configuration

Configure the pool on the cluster that hosts the storage:

  • Hyperconverged: the same cluster that will consume the storage.
  • Decoupled: the storage cluster (not the workload cluster).
ReplicatedErasure coded

Prefer this when you have fewer hosts or disks. Size 3 with failureDomain: host needs at least three servers with disks of the chosen device class.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephBlockPools:
          - name: "[pool-name]"
            spec:
              # Media for this pool. Valid values: hdd, ssd, nvme.
              # Device class is detected automatically on physical disks and must
              # match your failure domain. With failureDomain "host" and size 3,
              # you need three servers that each have disks of this class.
              deviceClass: hdd
              # Where replicas are placed. "host" spreads data across servers so
              # you can lose a machine. "osd" spreads across disks and may place
              # all copies on one server. Losing that server can mean permanent
              # data loss. With size 3 and failureDomain "host", you can lose
              # two hosts and still recover.
              failureDomain: "host"
              # Number of replicas across failure domains. With "host", size 3
              # means three different servers. Higher size uses more raw capacity
              # (1 TB usable ≈ 3 TB raw at size 3).
              replicated:
                size: 3
              # Per-disk RBD metrics in Prometheus. Recommended.
              enableRBDStats: true

Prefer this for large capacity once you have enough failure domains. We recommend 4+2 as a minimum (dataChunks: 4, codingChunks: 2): you need at least six servers when failureDomain is host, and you can lose two of them without data loss.

How erasure coding works

Each object is split into data chunks (k) and coding (parity) chunks (m). Any k of the k + m chunks can reconstruct the object, so you can lose up to m failure domains.

Storage overhead is: (dataChunks + codingChunks) / dataChunks

Examples:

Profile Fields Failure domains needed Can lose Raw for 1 TB usable 4+2 (recommended minimum) dataChunks: 4, codingChunks: 2 6 2 1.5 TB (50% overhead) 8+3 dataChunks: 8, codingChunks: 3 11 3 1.375 TB (~38% overhead) 2+1 (lab only) dataChunks: 2, codingChunks: 1 3 1 1.5 TB (50% overhead)

For comparison, 3× replication uses about 3 TB raw per 1 TB usable. Avoid profiles smaller than 4+2 in production: fewer coding chunks means less durability, and small k values leave little room to grow efficiency.

For block storage, Rook requires a replicated metadata pool plus an erasure-coded data pool. Configure that with cephECBlockPools:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephECBlockPools:
          - name: "[pool-name]"
            spec:
              # Replicated pool used for RBD image metadata.
              metadataPool:
                failureDomain: "host"
                replicated:
                  size: 3
              # Erasure-coded pool that holds the image data.
              dataPool:
                # Media for this pool. Valid values: hdd, ssd, nvme.
                deviceClass: hdd
                # Where EC chunks are placed. "host" spreads chunks across
                # servers so you can lose a machine. "osd" spreads across
                # disks and may place several chunks on one server. Losing
                # that server can exceed codingChunks and mean permanent
                # data loss. Prefer "host". You need dataChunks +
                # codingChunks failure domains (6 hosts for 4+2).
                failureDomain: "host"
                # k data chunks + m coding chunks. Overhead =
                # (k + m) / k. Recommend at least 4+2 in production.
                erasureCoded:
                  dataChunks: 4
                  codingChunks: 2

For advanced pool options, see the rook-ceph-cluster Helm chart values.

items.title: Replication
items.text:
Replication copies the pool's content to a pool on another storage cluster. The peer keeps the latest mirrored snapshot, so a failover can start from that export.

Replication has to be setup between pools, but is then enabled per project or per disk within a project. You don't have to synchronize the entire content of the pool.

Use it together with backups. A backup rebuilds a project, including its metadata, from the copy stored in S3. Restoring that copy is slower than attaching the latest replicated export, so replication is what keeps the recovery time objective (RTO) low.

Replication is asynchronous. Keep the backup as well: the peer holds the latest mirrored snapshot, and the backup the metadata and an history of the data over multiple days (depending on your retention).

Configure replication on both clusters that host the storage, in the same rook-local-cluster values as the pool:

  • The pool name is identical on both clusters. For an erasure-coded pool, that includes both Ceph pools, [pool-name] and [pool-name]-metadata.
  • The data protection and the device class can differ. One side can be a 3-replica NVMe pool while the other is an erasure-coded pool on HDD (to save on storage on the recovery cluster).
  • Mirroring is enabled on the pool on both clusters, and each cluster holds a secret that contains the other cluster's bootstrap token.
  • Each storage cluster runs at least one RBD mirror daemon.

items.title: Enable mirroring
items.text:
Add mirroring under the pool spec on both clusters. On an erasure-coded pool, add it only on the metadataPool and thedataPool will get automatically replicated.

mirroring:
  enabled: true
  # Mirror each RBD image, including its snapshots.
  mode: image

Rook then stores a bootstrap token in a Secret in the spx-storage namespace. Its name is reported on the pool:

kubectl -n spx-storage get cephblockpool [pool-name] \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.info.rbdMirrorBootstrapPeerSecretName}{"\n"}'

The Secret is usually named pool-peer-token-[pool-name]. Read the token:

kubectl -n spx-storage get secret pool-peer-token-[pool-name] \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 --decode; echo

items.title: Share the token
items.text:
On each cluster, create a Secret that holds the other cluster's token. [pool-name] is the pool name on this cluster, which is the same name as on the peer.

kubectl -n spx-storage create secret generic [peer-secret] \
  --from-literal=token='[token]' \
  --from-literal=pool='[pool-name]'

Point the pool at that Secret:

mirroring:
  enabled: true
  mode: image
  peers:
    # Secret in spx-storage that holds the other cluster's bootstrap token.
    secretNames:
      - "[peer-secret]"

Repeat in the other direction, so each pool lists the Secret that contains the remote token. For an erasure-coded pool, import a token and set peers.secretNames on both [pool-name] and [pool-name]-metadata.

items.title: Run the mirror daemon
items.text:
Apply this manifest on both storage clusters. One daemon is enough for the pools on that cluster. The Rook chart has no value for it, so apply the manifest directly.

apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephRBDMirror
metadata:
  name: rbd-mirror
  namespace: spx-storage
spec:
  # At least one daemon serves every mirrored pool on the cluster.
  count: 1

Check that the daemon is running:

kubectl -n spx-storage get pods -l app=rook-ceph-rbd-mirror

See the CephBlockPool mirroring reference for the full spec.

Expose the pool to tenants with a block storage class. On a decoupled AZ, connect the workload cluster first.

items.title: Adding an object store
items.text:
An object store is the Ceph RADOS Gateway (RGW) that serves the S3 API. Buckets created by tenants are stored there. Each store has:

  • A metadata pool. It holds the bucket index and the rest of the RGW metadata. It stays small next to the object data and is sensitive to latency, so SSD or NVMe is a good fit.
  • A data pool. It holds the objects. It can be replicated or erasure coded.
  • One or more gateway that serves the S3 API.

Superphenix ships with cephObjectStores empty, so a cluster has no object store until you add one. Add it on the cluster that hosts Ceph, then publish it to tenants with an object storage class.

Both pools use the same media, failure domain, and data protection as a storage pool. Follow that article for device classes, replication, and erasure coding, including the host counts each profile needs. Disks Rook is allowed to claim are set in Configuring the storage cluster. Add another object store when those choices should differ, for example an erasure-coded HDD store for capacity and a replicated NVMe store for latency.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Add the store under systemConfiguration on the Cluster resource (or via the superphenix-operator Helm chart), using the rook-local-cluster chart. Choose the example that matches the data pool. The metadata pool always uses the replicated layout.

Where to apply this configuration

Configure the object store on the cluster that hosts the storage:

  • Hyperconverged: the same cluster that will consume the storage.
  • Decoupled: the storage cluster (not the workload cluster).
ReplicatedErasure coded

Use this when the data pool should be replicated. The pool fields are the ones documented for a replicated storage pool.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephObjectStores:
          - name: "[object-store-name]"
            spec:
              metadataPool:
                # RGW metadata. Always replicated. See "Adding a storage pool".
                # We recommend SSD/NVMes here, but can also be HDD
                deviceClass: ssd
                failureDomain: "host"
                replicated:
                  size: 3
              dataPool:
                # Object data. Same fields as a replicated storage pool.
                deviceClass: hdd
                failureDomain: "host"
                replicated:
                  size: 3
              # Keep the pools if this object store is deleted, so the objects
              # remain. Set false only when you intend to drop the data with the store.
              preservePoolsOnDelete: true
              gateway:
                # HTTP port on which the store will listen.
                port: 8090
                # Number of gateways we'll deploy. The more we have, the more traffic we can
                # ingress. Any node of the cluster can act as a gateway.
                instances: 3
            # Tenant-facing classes are created with rook-connection.
            # Leave the chart's own bucket class disabled.
            storageClass:
              enabled: false
            # The ingress to expose the storage class and make every node respond to S3 traffic.
            # Traefik terminates TLS and forwards to the gateway port.
            ingress:
              enabled: true
              annotations:
                cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "0"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-request-buffering: "off"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTP"
              host:
                # Public S3 hostname. Point DNS at the cluster.
                name: s3.example.org
                path: /
              tls:
                - hosts:
                    - s3.example.org
                  secretName: "[object-store-name]-tls"

Use this when the data pool should be erasure coded. The data pool fields are the ones documented for an erasure-coded storage pool. The metadata pool stays replicated.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephObjectStores:
          - name: "[object-store-name]"
            spec:
              metadataPool:
                # RGW metadata. Always replicated, including when object data is erasure coded.
                # See "Adding a storage pool".
                # We recommend SSD/NVMes here, but can also be HDD
                deviceClass: ssd
                failureDomain: "host"
                replicated:
                  size: 3
              dataPool:
                # Object data. Same fields as an erasure-coded storage pool.
                deviceClass: hdd
                failureDomain: "host"
                erasureCoded:
                  dataChunks: 4
                  codingChunks: 2
              # Keep the pools if this object store is deleted, so the objects
              # remain. Set false only when you intend to drop the data with the store.
              preservePoolsOnDelete: true
              gateway:
                # HTTP port on which the store will listen.
                port: 8090
                # Number of gateways we'll deploy. The more we have, the more traffic we can
                # ingress. Any node of the cluster can act as a gateway.
                instances: 3
            # Tenant-facing classes are created with rook-connection.
            # Leave the chart's own bucket class disabled.
            storageClass:
              enabled: false
            # The ingress to expose the storage class and make every node respond to S3 traffic.
            # Traefik terminates TLS and forwards to the gateway port.
            ingress:
              enabled: true
              annotations:
                cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "0"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-request-buffering: "off"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
                nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTP"
              host:
                # Public S3 hostname. Point DNS at the cluster.
                name: s3.example.org
                path: /
              tls:
                - hosts:
                    - s3.example.org
                  secretName: "[object-store-name]-tls"

The name is the CephObjectStore name on this cluster. Use that same [object-store-name] when you add an object storage class.

The Ingress is the S3 endpoint clients use (https://s3.example.org). Replace the hostname and point DNS at the nodes of the cluster. Any node of the cluster is capable of handling S3.

For advanced pool and gateway options, see the rook-ceph-cluster Helm chart values.

items.title: Verify the object store
items.text:
The store is created in the rook-local-cluster namespace, spx-storage. Wait until its phase is Ready and one gateway pod is running for each gateway.instances:

kubectl -n spx-storage get cephobjectstore
kubectl -n spx-storage get pods -l app=rook-ceph-rgw

Then expose the store to tenants:

  • Hyperconverged: add an object storage class on this cluster.
  • Decoupled: connect the workload cluster, then add the object storage class there.

items.title: Configuring backups
items.text:
A backup is a copy of a project stored in S3. It includes the project's metadata and its data, so the project can be rebuilt from an empty availability zone. Backups can be partial (a VM, an application) or full (the entire content of the project).

Users can create backups by themselves, and set schedules to do periodic backups with a custom retention. Configure a backup location on every AZ. Until that location exists, backups on the AZ fail.

Backups are the recovery copy used in two cases:

  • Disaster recovery across availability zones. One AZ fails, and another AZ restores the project from the backups it has been receiving.
  • A restore on the AZ that created the backup, using the remote copy.

Snapshots stay on the cluster and protect disks locally. Backups leave the cluster. For a shorter recovery of the disks themselves, enable block pool replication. Starting from the latest replicated export is faster than restoring a backup.

items.title: Where the backups go
items.text:
The destination is an S3 bucket. It can be:

  • An object store on another Superphenix cluster. Place it far from the AZ that produces the backups, on a path that stays fast when many backups run at once.
  • An S3 endpoint outside Superphenix.
  • An object store on the same cluster. Prefer a remote bucket. Snapshots already cover local data protection, and a bucket on the same cluster is lost with the cluster.

With two AZs, cross the destinations: AZ A writes to a bucket on AZ B, and AZ B writes to a bucket on AZ A.

The location marked as the default is where this AZ's backups are written. Add further locations when this AZ should restore from backups that another AZ produced. How to run that restore will be covered in a disaster recovery article. That article is not published yet.

Where to apply this configuration

Set the backup location on the cluster that runs workloads:

  • Hyperconverged: the AZ cluster.
  • Decoupled: the workload cluster (not the storage cluster).

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Add the location under systemConfiguration on the Cluster resource (or via the superphenix-operator Helm chart), using the velero chart.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    velero:
      values:
        configuration:
          # S3 bucket that receives this AZ's backups.
          backupStorageLocation:
            - name: "[location name]"
              # Only one location can have this property.
              # This is where Superphenix will send the backups.
              default: true
              provider: aws
              bucket: "[bucket name]"
              prefix: velero
              config:
                # Identifier for the bucket's region. When AZs cross backups,
                # use the name of the AZ that hosts the bucket.
                region: "[az name]"
                s3Url: https://s3.example.org
                s3ForcePathStyle: true
            # Restore source only. Backups are written to the default location above.
            # - name: "[remote az]"
            #   default: false
            #   accessMode: ReadOnly
            #   provider: aws
            #   bucket: "[bucket name]"
            #   prefix: velero
            #   config:
            #     region: "[az name]"
            #     s3Url: https://s3.other.example.org
            #     s3ForcePathStyle: true
        # Credentials for the S3 bucket. The secretContents key is "cloud".
        # The profile heading matches backupStorageLocation.name.
        credentials:
          secretContents:
            cloud: |
              [location name]
              aws_access_key_id=[access key]
              aws_secret_access_key=[secret key]
            # [remote az]
            # aws_access_key_id=[access key]
            # aws_secret_access_key=[secret key]
  • backupStorageLocation[].name: name of this location
  • default: set on the location backups are written to. One location on the AZ is the default.
  • bucket and prefix: bucket name, and the path inside it (velero).
  • config.region: region identifier sent to S3. For a bucket on the opposite AZ, use that AZ's name.
  • config.s3Url: S3 endpoint, for example the object store hostname from Adding an object store.
  • secretContents.cloud: credentials file for the backup location. The profile heading, [location name], is the backup location name. The keys need read and write access to the bucket.
  • accessMode: ReadOnly: use this on extra locations. Those locations are restore sources and do not receive this AZ's backups.

For advanced options, see the Velero Helm chart values.

items.title: Configuring the storage cluster
items.text:
Configure the storage cluster through the rook-local-cluster chart under systemConfiguration on the cluster that hosts Ceph. Applying configuration changes is how that values file is upgraded. The same pattern applies to both hyperconverged and decoupled deployments.

The parameters below are the ones changed most often: Ceph network address ranges and which disks Rook claims for OSDs.

Where to apply this configuration

Configure storage on the cluster that hosts Ceph:

  • Hyperconverged: the single AZ cluster (storage and workloads together).
  • Decoupled: the storage cluster (not the workload cluster).
systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephClusterSpec:
          network:
            addressRanges:
              public:
                - fd00:ffff:2000::/64
              cluster:
                - fd00:ffff:2001::/96
          storage:
            deviceFilter: "nvme*|sd*"
  • network.addressRanges.public: address range for Ceph client (public) traffic.
  • network.addressRanges.cluster: address range for Ceph replication and recovery traffic. Keep node addresses within the reserved range.
  • storage.deviceFilter: which disks Rook claims as OSDs (for example NVMe and SCSI disks matching nvme* or sd*).

For advanced options, see the rook-ceph-cluster Helm chart values.

items.title: Connecting a workload and storage cluster
items.text:
In a decoupled AZ, storage and workloads run on separate Superphenix clusters. Before a workload cluster can expose block or object storage classes to tenants, you must connect it to one or more storage clusters.

The relationship is many-to-many:

  • One workload cluster can connect to many storage clusters.
  • One storage cluster can be consumed by many workload clusters.

This article applies only to decoupled deployments. On hyperconverged clusters, storage and workloads already share the same cluster, so no cross-cluster connection is required.

Create the Ceph accounts on the storage cluster, in the spx-storage namespace. Then apply the connection under systemConfiguration on the workload Cluster resource (or via the superphenix-operator Helm chart), using the rook-connection chart.
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Consuming block storage
items.text:
Connect the workload cluster to a storage cluster so it can consume Ceph block pools. After the connection is in place, expose pools to tenants with block storage classes.

Block access uses two Ceph clients on the storage cluster:

  • csi-health checks cluster health and refreshes the monitor list.
  • A pool client is what the workload cluster uses to provision and attach RBD volumes. Create one client per workload cluster.
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: CSI health account
items.text:
Apply this on the storage cluster:

apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephClient
metadata:
  name: csi-health
  namespace: spx-storage
spec:
  caps:
    mon: "allow r, allow command quorum_status, allow command version"

Rook creates the Ceph user client.csi-health and stores its key in the Secret rook-ceph-client-csi-health. That key is the health-check token:

kubectl -n spx-storage get secret rook-ceph-client-csi-health \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.csi-health}' | base64 --decode
echo
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Pool client
items.text:
Apply a CephClient on the storage cluster. [name] is the client name you choose for this workload cluster. Rook creates the Ceph user client.[name] and the Secret rook-ceph-client-[name].

The same pool list goes on both mgr and osd. Each entry is profile rbd pool=<ceph-pool-name>. The name is the CephBlockPool name (kubectl -n spx-storage get cephblockpool). An erasure-coded pool is two Ceph pools. If you followed Adding a storage pool, those names are [pool-name]-metadata and [pool-name].

Selected poolsEntire cluster

List only the pools this workload cluster may use:

apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephClient
metadata:
  name: "[name]"
  namespace: spx-storage
spec:
  caps:
    mon: "profile rbd"
    # One "profile rbd pool=<name>" entry per Ceph pool, on both mgr and osd.
    mgr: "profile rbd pool=[pool-name], profile rbd pool=[ec-pool-name]-metadata, profile rbd pool=[ec-pool-name]"
    osd: "profile rbd pool=[pool-name], profile rbd pool=[ec-pool-name]-metadata, profile rbd pool=[ec-pool-name]"

Omit every pool= directive to grant this client access to every pool on the storage cluster:

apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephClient
metadata:
  name: "[name]"
  namespace: spx-storage
spec:
  caps:
    mon: "profile rbd"
    mgr: "profile rbd"
    osd: "profile rbd"

Read the key after the client is ready. This key is the connection token. The connection username is the CephClient name, without the client. prefix:

kubectl -n spx-storage get secret rook-ceph-client-[name] \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.[name]}' | base64 --decode
echo
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Connect the workload cluster
items.text:
Apply this on the workload cluster. Retrieve the remaining connection values from the remote storage cluster as follows:

  • clusterID: from .status.cephClusters on the Superphenix Cluster CR for the remote storage cluster. The Ceph FSID is the key of that dictionary (for example e2a62ea1-6428-496e-a5bf-366936a8c833).
  • username: the pool client's CephClient name ([name]), without the client. prefix.
  • token: the key from Secret rook-ceph-client-[name].
  • bootstrapMon: the public address of one Ceph monitor on the storage cluster (id, ip, port, and protocol). It is used only to bootstrap the connection. After that, the full MON list is pulled and kept fresh; this bootstrap MON is not used again.
  • healthCheck.username: client.csi-health.
  • healthCheck.token: the key from Secret rook-ceph-client-csi-health.
systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-connection:
      values:
        clusters:
          - name: "[storage-cluster-name]" # The name of the remote storage cluster
            # From .status.cephClusters on the remote Cluster CR (dictionary key = FSID)
            clusterID: ""
            # CephClient name of the pool client, without the client. prefix
            username: "[name]"
            # Key from Secret rook-ceph-client-[name] on the storage cluster
            token: ""
            # Public address of one MON; used only to bootstrap, then the full MON list is refreshed
            bootstrapMon:
              # MON ID (must be a single letter)
              id: ""
              # IP of the MON
              ip: ""
              # Port of the MON
              port: "6789"
              # Protocol of the IP (IPv4 or IPv6)
              protocol: IPv6
            # client.csi-health, and the key from Secret rook-ceph-client-csi-health
            healthCheck:
              username: "client.csi-health"
              token: ""
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Consuming object storage
items.text: Connect the workload cluster to a storage cluster so it can consume an RGW object store. After the connection is in place, expose the store to tenants with object storage classes.
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Create the admin user
items.text:
Apply a CephObjectStoreUser on the storage cluster, one per object store. The user name matches the store name. displayName is the RGW display name. The capabilities below let the workload cluster manage buckets and read usage for that store.

apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephObjectStoreUser
metadata:
  name: "[store]"
  namespace: spx-storage
spec:
  store: "[store]"
  displayName: "admin"
  capabilities:
    bucket: "*"
    users: "*"
    usage: "read"
    metadata: "read"
    zone: "read"

[store] is the CephObjectStore name from Adding an object store. Rook stores the S3 keys in the Secret rook-ceph-object-user-[store]-[store]:

kubectl -n spx-storage get secret rook-ceph-object-user-[store]-[store] \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.AccessKey}' | base64 --decode
echo
kubectl -n spx-storage get secret rook-ceph-object-user-[store]-[store] \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.SecretKey}' | base64 --decode
echo

AccessKey is rgwAdminOps.accessKey. SecretKey is rgwAdminOps.secretKey.
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Connect the workload cluster
items.text:
Apply this on the workload cluster:

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-connection:
      values:
        clusters:
          - name: "[storage-cluster-name]" # The name of the remote storage cluster
            # Keys from Secret rook-ceph-object-user-[store]-[store] on the storage cluster
            rgwAdminOps:
              accessKey: ""
              secretKey: ""
            objectStores:
              - name: "[object-store-name]" # CephObjectStore CR name (also used to derive the TLS secret name)
                # External RGW endpoints. Each entry accepts either `ip` or `hostname`.
                endpoints:
                  - hostname: "s3.example.org"
                    # ip: ""
                # Gateway HTTP port
                port: 80
                # Gateway HTTPS port (only set when TLS is enabled)
                # securePort: 443
                # TLS configuration for the remote RGW
                # tls:
                #   enabled: false
                #   # PEM-encoded certificate the operator will trust when talking to the RGW
                #   cert: ""

For advanced connection options, see the spx-rook-connection chart values.
path: Connecting a workload and storage cluster

items.title: Enabling block pool replication
items.text:
Block pool replication copies RBD images from one storage cluster to another. The peer keeps the latest mirrored snapshot, so a failover can start from that export.

Use it together with backups. A backup rebuilds a project, including its metadata, from the copy stored in S3. Restoring that copy is slower than attaching the latest replicated export, so replication is what keeps the recovery time objective (RTO) low.

Replication is asynchronous. Keep the backup as well: the peer holds the latest mirrored snapshot, and it can be a few snapshots behind the source.

Where to apply this

Apply the pool and the mirror daemon on the cluster that hosts the storage, on both sides of the replication:

  • Hyperconverged — the AZ
  • Decoupled — the storage cluster

The pool is configured through the rook-local-cluster application, in the same place as adding a storage pool.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• The pool name is identical on both clusters. For an erasure-coded pool, that includes both Ceph pools, [pool-name] and [pool-name]-metadata.
  • The data protection and the device class can differ. One side can be a 3-replica NVMe pool while the other is an erasure-coded pool on HDD.
  • Mirroring is enabled on the pool on both clusters, and each cluster holds a secret that contains the other cluster's bootstrap token.
  • Each storage cluster runs one RBD mirror daemon.

items.title: Enable mirroring
items.text:
Add mirroring to the pool spec on both clusters. The example below is the replicated pool from adding a storage pool; only the mirroring section is new.

systemConfiguration:
  apps:
    rook-local-cluster:
      values:
        cephBlockPools:
          - name: "[pool-name]"
            spec:
              failureDomain: host
              replicated:
                size: 3
              deviceClass: "nvme"
              mirroring:
                enabled: true
                mode: image

On an erasure-coded pool, add the same mirroring block only under the metadataPool. The dataPool will automatically get replicated if its metadataPool is replicated.

Once mirroring is enabled, Rook stores a bootstrap token in a Secret in the spx-storage namespace. Its name is reported on the pool:

kubectl -n spx-storage get cephblockpool [pool-name] \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.info.rbdMirrorBootstrapPeerSecretName}{"\n"}'

The Secret is usually named pool-peer-token-[pool-name]. Read the token:

kubectl -n spx-storage get secret pool-peer-token-[pool-name] \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 --decode; echo

items.title: Share the token
items.text:
On each cluster, create a Secret that holds the other cluster's token. [pool-name] is the pool name on this cluster, which is the same name as on the peer.

kubectl -n spx-storage create secret generic [peer-secret] \
  --from-literal=token='[token]' \
  --from-literal=pool='[pool-name]'

Point the pool at that Secret:

mirroring:
  enabled: true
  mode: image
  peers:
    secretNames:
      - "[peer-secret]"

Repeat in the other direction, so each pool lists the Secret that contains the remote token. For an erasure-coded pool, import a token and set peers.secretNames on both [pool-name] and [pool-name]-metadata.

items.title: Run the mirror daemon
items.text:
Apply this manifest on both storage clusters. One daemon is enough for the pools on that cluster.

apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephRBDMirror
metadata:
  name: rbd-mirror
  namespace: spx-storage
spec:
  count: 1

Check that the daemon is running:

kubectl -n spx-storage get pods -l app=rook-ceph-rbd-mirror

items.title: Fields
items.text:
Field Description mirroring.enabled Turns on RBD mirroring for the pool. Set it on both clusters. mirroring.mode image mirrors each RBD image, including its snapshots. mirroring.peers.secretNames Secrets in spx-storage that contain a remote cluster's bootstrap token. CephRBDMirror.spec.count Number of mirror daemons. 1 serves every mirrored pool on the cluster.

For the full pool spec, see the CephBlockPool reference.

items.title: Using local storage
items.text:
Superphenix normally uses Ceph to provide replicated network storage. For debugging on hardware with slow disks, Ceph replication and network overhead can make storage perform poorly. You can instead enable the local path provisioner and store volumes directly on each node.

Debugging only

Local storage is not resilient. Losing the node or its disk means losing the data stored there. A workload using a local volume is also tied to that node and cannot be rescheduled elsewhere while retaining its data. Do not use this configuration for production data.

items.title: Enable local storage
items.text:
Enable local-path-provisioner in the cluster's system configuration. For the local hyperconverged cluster configured through the superphenix-operator Helm values, use:

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        local-path-provisioner:
          enabled: true

items.title: Disable Ceph and use only local storage
items.text:
For a disposable debugging cluster, you can disable Ceph cluster and make local-path the default storage class. The local path provisioner chart uses storageClass.defaultClass for this setting:

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        rook-operator:
          enabled: false
        rook-local-cluster:
          enabled: false
        rook-connection:
          enabled: false
        local-path-provisioner:
          enabled: true
          values:
            storageClass:
              defaultClass: true

With this configuration, persistent volume claims that do not specify storageClassName use local-path.

Do not switch a cluster that contains data

Disabling Ceph does not migrate existing volumes to local storage. Ceph-backed workloads may stop working, and their data may become unavailable. Use this configuration only when creating or resetting a disposable debugging cluster.

items.title: Verify the storage class
items.text:
Wait for the application to become healthy, then confirm that Kubernetes exposes the local-path storage class:

kubectl get storageclass

The output marks local-path as (default) when storageClass.defaultClass is enabled. The provisioner creates a volume on the node where its consuming workload is scheduled.

items.title: Use local storage
items.text:
We can now use the local-path storage class instead of the default one. For example, we can make the Kubernetes as a Service etcd datastores use the local disks:

clusters:
  local:
    systemConfiguration:
      apps:
        kaas-datastore:
          values:
            dataStores:
              default:
                storageClassName: local-path

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• No redundancy: the data has a single copy on one local disk.
  • No node failover: if the node is unavailable, the workload cannot start on another node with the same data.
  • No disk-failure recovery: replacing or losing the disk loses its local volumes.
  • Not shared storage: local volumes are unsuitable for workloads that require storage accessible from multiple nodes.

Use the local-path storage class only for disposable debugging workloads. Use Ceph-backed storage classes for persistent or production workloads.

items.title: Kubernetes as a service on Superphenix
items.text: Superphenix is designed to offer Kubernetes as a Service (KaaS) so tenants can run managed Kubernetes clusters on the same virtualization, storage, and network stack as your IaaS workloads.

items.title: VM pools (worker nodes)
items.text:
Tenant clusters are backed by pools of VMs where you define:

  • VM sizing: CPU, memory, and disk for control-plane and worker machines.
  • Networking: Node pools are attached to your VPCs and subnets; pods and services use the integrated CNI on top of that underlay.

items.title: Platform integration
items.text: Capability Behavior CNI Integrated CNI: cluster networking is provided by the platform stack (same SDN as VMs where applicable). CSI Integrated CSI: persistent volumes map to the platform storage layer. Live migration Worker VMs can be live-migrated like any other instance when policy allows, for node maintenance without hard downtime for stateless workloads. Disaster recovery Controlplane data and worker nodes can be backed up and replicated allowing for quick recovery in case of outages or catastrophic failure.

items.title: Operations
items.text:
• Create, scale, upgrade, and delete clusters via GitOps and console.
  • Use the same organization / project RBAC as the rest of the platform; see Organizations and projects.

items.title: Foundation used
items.text: Foundation How Kubernetes uses it Virtualization VM pools for nodes (Compute) Network VPCs, subnets, NAT, LB, firewall (Network) Storage CSI-backed volumes (Storage)

items.title: Version support
items.text: Each version of Superphenix will support 3 minor Kubernetes versions at a time. You may encounter different supported versions for a single Superphenix deployment as some AZs might be more up to date than others.

items.title: Advanced configuration
items.text: To accommodate for more specific needs, KaaS clusters support a range of additionnal configuration options.

items.title: Essential cluster components
items.text:
You can override the default configuration of the following components of your cluster:

  • CoreDNS
  • CNI: Cilium
  • Metrics server

The default configuration can be found here: kaas-essentials

Here is how you can achieve this:

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under Advanced Configuration → Cluster Essentials Customization, click on Edit config for the given component and write the configuration overrides in the pop-up window. Expected input are values from the component's Helm chart in YAML format.

For example, to change the amount of CoreDNS replicas you would write: 

replicaCount: 1

  1. Add your custom Helm values under <cluster-name>.kaasEssentials.values.<coredns/cilium/metrics-server>.

For example, to change the amount of CoreDNS replicas you would have: 

my-cluster:
  kaasEssentials:
    values:
      coredns:
        replicaCount: 1

Full chart values: sfs-kaas.

items.title: Post-installation Helm chart
items.text:
You can further automate the setup process of your cluster by pointing to a custom Helm chart which will be applied to the cluster during the installation.

To accomplish this follow these steps:

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under Advanced Configuration, enable the Post Installation Chart toggle
  4. Fill out the information about the desired chart:
    • Chart Name
    • Chart Version
    • Namespace: target namespace where the chart should be applied.
    • Repository URL: Source reposistory to pull the chart from.
  5. Click on Helm Chart Values → Edit values and write the configuration overrides for you chart.
  1. Add deployment specification about your chart under <cluster-name>.postInstallChart:
    • chartName
    • chartVersion
    • namespace: target namespace where the chart should be applied.
    • repoUrl: Source reposistory to pull the chart from.
    • revision: Counter that needs to be increased to trigger the re-apply of the chart.

Example for the Traefik ingress and gatewayAPI controller: 

my-cluster:
  postInstallChart:
    chartName: traefik
    chartVersion: 39.0.2
    repoUrl: https://traefik.github.io/charts
    revision: 1
    values:
      # add your values here

Full chart values: sfs-kaas.

items.title: Basic operations
items.text: This section details the most common actions regarding Kubernetes clusters on Superphenix: deploying, scaling, upgrading and deleting.

items.title: Deploying a cluster
items.text:
Requirements

KaaS cluster nodes are deployed in the same VPC and subnet as any IaaS virtual machines, but their controlplane runs inside a separate VPC which means that the nodes will reach out over the world wide web to access it. Therefore, make sure that your subnet has internet access when creating a cluster. This can be achieved by creating an EIP with the SNAT option enabled and attaching it to your subnet.

To deploy a cluster through the console, follow the steps of the creation wizard. For a GitOps deployment, you can copy and adjust the example below based on your needs.

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Open PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Create Cluster (top right).
  3. Under General Information set:
    • Name
    • AZ: must match where you want the cluster to be deployed.
    • Cluster Version: Kubernetes version.
  4. Optionally, you can:
    • Enable Advanced configuration options.
    • Enable Disaster Recovery.
    • Configure the Cluster Network Policies.
  5. Under Cluster Instance Group, create one or more node groups, for each of them set:
    • Number of replicas: How many nodes should be created for this group.
    • Cores: Amount of vCPUs per node.
    • RAM: Memory quantity per node.
    • Storage Class: Storage type to use for the node's disks.
    • Boot disk size: Size of the node's disks.
  6. Under Network Configuration, add one or more subnets to each node group. (Nodes need to talk to each other and should therefore share at least one common subnet between all node groups).
  7. Click Create (bottom right).
my-cluster:
  name: "my-cluster"
  location: "my-az"
  # The list of supported versions for your AZ can be found in the console's creation wizard
  kubeVersion: v1.36.3 
  workers:
    instances:
      node-group-1:
        deployment:
          replicas: 2
        template:
          version: 1
          cores: 2
          memory: 4Gi
          interfaces:
            - subnet: "<my-subnet>"
          bootDisk:
            storage: 20Gi
  kaasEssentials:
    storageClasses:
      default:
        isDefaultClass: true
        tenantClass: default
        infraClass: default
    snapshotClasses:
      default:
        tenantClass: default
        infraClass: default

Full chart values: sfs-kaas.

Accessing your cluster

Once your cluster is ready, you can download its kubeconfig file from the console:

  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Download kubeconfig (top right).

items.title: Horizontal scaling
items.text:
Steps to add nodes to your cluster:

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under Cluster Instance Group you can either:
    • Increase the Number of replicas field of existing node groups.
    • Create new node groups using the Add Group button. Refer to the Deploying a cluster section for details.
  4. If you created new node groups, remember to assign them one or more subnets under the Network Configuration tab.
  5. Navigate to the last tab (Network Configuration) and click Update (bottom right).
  1. Increase <cluster-name>.workers.instances.<node-group>.deployment.replicas.
  2. Commit and push the changes.
  3. Go to the your project's page on the selfservice ArgoCD and synchronize the changes.

You can also create a new worker pool by adding its specification under <cluster-name>.workers.instances like in this example: 

node-group-2:
  deployment:
    replicas: 2
  template:
    version: 1
    cores: 2
    memory: 4Gi
    interfaces:
      - subnet: "<my-subnet>"
    bootDisk:
      storage: 30Gi

items.title: Vertical scaling
items.text:
Steps to increase the size of nodes in an existing node group. This will trigger a rolling update for the given node groups and create new nodes with the updated specification.

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under Cluster Instance Group, increase the amount of Cores, RAM or adjust the Boot disk size as needed for each node group.
  4. Navigate to the last tab (Network Configuration) and click Update (bottom right).
  1. Update <cluster-name>.workers.instances.<node-group>.template.cores, .memory or .bootDisk.storage as desired.
  2. Increment <cluster-name>.workers.instances.<node-group>.template.version. This is required for the specification update to take effect.
  3. Commit and push the changes.
  4. Go to the your project's page on the selfservice ArgoCD and synchronize the changes.
Rolling update configuration

You can control how the rolling update process behaves by setting <cluster-name>.workers.instances.<node-group>.template.maxSurge and .maxUnavailable.

Example: 

node-group-1:
  deployment:
    replicas: 2
  template:
    version: 2 # <-- Increment to trigger node rolling update
    cores: 4
    memory: 12Gi
    interfaces:
      - subnet: "<my-subnet>"
    bootDisk:
      storage: 30Gi

items.title: Upgrading a cluster
items.text:
To upgrade your cluster, follow these steps to trigger a controlplane upgrade. Once it is done the worker VMs will undergo a rolling update.

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under General information, pick a new Cluster Version from the list.
  4. Navigate to the last tab (Network Configuration) and click Update (bottom right).
  1. Change <cluster-name>.kubeVersion to the desired version.
  2. Commit and push the changes.
  3. Go to the your project's page on the selfservice ArgoCD and synchronize the changes.
Rolling update configuration

You can control how the rolling update process behaves by setting <cluster-name>.workers.instances.<node-group>.template.maxSurge and .maxUnavailable.

items.title: Deleting a cluster
items.text:
To delete a cluster, procceed as described:

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Delete (top right).
  3. In the pop-up window, double check the cluster's name and click Confirm.
  1. Remove the cluster specification from your repository.
  2. Access your cluster's application page on the selfservice ArgoCD and click the Delete button in the top row.
  3. In the pop-up window, double check the cluster's name and click OK.

items.title: Disaster recovery
items.text: Depending on the criticity of your workloads, you may want to be able to restore your cluster in case of catastrophic failure, or have the option to migrate it to a different AZ in case of a major outage.

items.title: Enabling disaster recovery
items.text:
Follow this guide to enable the disaster recovery option on your cluster. This makes it possible to include it in project-scoped backups.

Backup creation

Enabling the disaster recovery option will not automatically create a corresponding backup schedule. You have to manually create a project-wide backup or backup schedule.

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under General Information, enable the Disaster Recovery switch.
  4. Navigate to the last tab (Network Configuration) and click Update (bottom right).
  1. Enable and configure the dedicated datastore option under <cluster-name>.controlPlane.dataStore:
    • dedicated: Set to true to enable the disaster recovery option.
    • storageClassName: Storage type to use, as etcd clusters are latency sensitive, SSD-backed storage classes are best suited for this usecase.
    • storage: Size of the PVCs for the etcd members (Default value is 8Gi).

Example: 

my-cluster:
  controlPlane
    dataStore:
      dedicated: true
      storageClassName: default
      storage: 8Gi

Full chart values: sfs-kaas.

Enabling this functionality will create a dedicated etcd cluster and migrate the controlplane data to it. During the migration process the controlplane will become read-only, a migration typically only takes a few minutes.

Post migration

Once the controlplane is migrated to the dedicated datastore, complete the operation by rebooting your worker nodes via the console.

items.title: Restoring or migrating a cluster
items.text:
Performing a DR

Cluster migration and restoration can currently only be performed by Superphenix admins.

items.title: Node subnets
items.text:
Worker nodes need to talk to each other and therefore need at least one shared subnet between all node groups. You can than add more subnets to certain node groups depending on your needs.

Internal cluster CIDRs

By default KaaS clusters use the following IP ranges:

  1. Pod CIDR:
    • 10.0.0.0/12
    • fd00:100::/96
  2. Service CIDR:
    • 10.96.0.0/16
    • fd00:100:ffff::/112

To avoid issues your node's subnet CIDR should not overlap with the pod CIDR.

items.title: Network policies
items.text:
Work in progress

The cluster networkpolicies configuration is currently beeing reworked, documentation will be updated accrodingly once done.

items.title: Default policies
items.text:
By default a KaaS cluster installation will deploy networkPolicies which ensure that:

  • Controlplane is joinable from anywhere.
  • Communication between worker nodes is allowed.
  • Nodes can access the internet.
  • Nodes can be accessed from anywhere.

items.title: Customize the configuration
items.text:
Known limitations

Currently this mechanism cannot be used to limit controlplane access to a specific range of public IPs.

You can control the networkPolicies for the controlplane and worker nodes independently:

ConsoleGitOps
  1. Access your cluster's page under PaaS → Kubernetes.
  2. Click Options → Edit (top right).
  3. Under General Information → Cluster Network Policies you can set:
    • Control Plane Network Policies to either default or none (Default allows ingress from anywhere).
    • Workers Network Policies to default, strict or none (Default allows communications from and to anywhere, Strict limits ingress to other nodes of the same cluster).
  4. Navigate to the last tab (Network Configuration) and click Update (bottom right).
my-cluster:
  controlPlane:
    network:
      defaultPolicies: default/none
  workers:
    network:
      defaultPolicies: default/strict/none

Full chart values: sfs-kaas.

Disabling those networkPolicies allows you to define your own security groups to restrict traffic to and from the cluster. These are the labels you can use to target the cluster components in your rules:

  1. Controlplane 
    superphenix.net/resourceEffectiveID: <SPXID of your cluster>
superphenix.net/workloadClass: kaas-tenant-api-server
  2. Worker nodes 
    cluster.x-k8s.io/cluster-name: <SPXID of your cluster>

items.title: Reference
items.text:
Field-level reference for the Superphenix custom resources, the HTTP APIs, and the Helm charts that install and configure the platform.

This section is useful for configuration values and learning how to automate tasks through the Superphenix API.

  • CRDs

    Custom resources for clusters, organizations, and projects.

    CRDs

  • OpenAPI

    Swagger documents for the API and the per-AZ controller.

    OpenAPI

  • Helm charts

    Chart values and the documentation that ships with each chart.

    Helm charts

items.title: CRDs
items.text:
Superphenix registers three namespaced custom resources in the group operator.superphenix.net/v1alpha1. The Go types live in api/operator/v1alpha1/ of the Superphenix repository. The operator chart installs the rendered CRDs from components/system/superphenix-operator/crds/.

Kind Plural Namespaced Role Cluster clusters ✓ One Superphenix cluster: topology, geography, connection, and lifecycle. Organization organizations ✓ A tenant organization onboarded through GitOps. Project projects ✓ A project inside an organization, including the availability zones where it may run.

All three are namespaced, and all three expose a status subresource. Create them in the namespace where the operator runs, typically superphenix-system.

items.title: Cluster
items.text:
A Cluster is one Superphenix Kubernetes cluster. The operator uses it to connect to that cluster and to install the Superphenix stack on it.

Group operator.superphenix.net Version v1alpha1 Kind Cluster Plural clusters Scope Namespaced

An install example is in Configure a cluster. Talos provisioning values passed through spec.talosManagerConfiguration are documented on the talos-manager chart. Values passed through spec.systemConfiguration are the superphenix-system chart.

items.title: Spec
items.text: Field Type Required Default Description deploymentTopology string No Hyperconverged or Decoupled. Leave it empty only for a management cluster. type string Conditional Storage, Workload, or Management. See the rules below. talosManagementMode string No Unmanaged How Talos is managed. Unmanaged, Import, or Full. talosManagerConfiguration object No Arbitrary YAML passed to the talos-manager chart. region string Yes Geographic region. At least one character. availabilityZone string Yes Availability zone identifier within the region. At least one character. systemConfiguration object No Arbitrary YAML passed to the superphenix-system chart. systemLocation object No Override for where the system chart is loaded. See below. version string No Controller default Superphenix version for this cluster. Must be a semantic version, with an optional v prefix. connection object Yes How the operator reaches the cluster. See below. lifecycle object No Pause, manual sync, and deletion behavior. See below.

items.title: Topology rules
items.text:
• When deploymentTopology is empty, type must be Management.
  • When deploymentTopology is Decoupled, type must be Storage or Workload.
  • Hyperconverged runs storage and workload on the same cluster. Decoupled splits them. Management is the cluster that runs the operator, and it has no deployment topology.

items.title: talosManagementMode
items.text: Value Meaning Unmanaged Talos is installed and configured outside the operator. Import The operator imports a Talos cluster that is already installed and then manages its configuration. Full The operator installs and configures Talos.

items.title: systemLocation
items.text: Field Type Description repoURL string Repository that hosts the superphenix-system chart. Empty uses the controller default. chartName string Chart name. Empty uses the controller default.

items.title: connection
items.text:
Field Type Required Default Description mode string Yes Local Remote or Local. url string When mode is Remote API server address of the remote cluster. Ignored when mode is Local. secretRef.name string When secretRef is set Name of the Secret that holds the connection credentials. secretRef.namespace string No Cluster namespace Namespace of that Secret.

Local means the cluster is the one where the operator is running. Remote connects with url and secretRef.

items.title: lifecycle
items.text: Field Type Default Description pause boolean false Pause synchronization. The operator adds an Argo CD sync window so automated and manual sync both stop. manual boolean false Disable autosync of every application on this cluster by passing forceManual to the system chart. cleanupOnDeletion boolean false On delete, cascade-delete applications on the target cluster. Turn this on only when a deletion is planned.

items.title: Status
items.text:
Field Type Description phase string Deployed, Deploying, OutOfSync, Error, Paused, or Unknown. superphenixVersion string Superphenix version currently running on the cluster. kubernetesVersion string Kubernetes version of the cluster. nodeCount integer Number of nodes. apps map Applications deployed by the cluster's root app-of-apps, keyed by application name. apps.<name>.name string Application name. apps.<name>.status string Health, such as Healthy, Degraded, or Progressing. apps.<name>.lastRefresh time Last time Argo CD reconciled the application against its source. apps.<name>.lastSync time Last time a sync of that application completed. apps.<name>.version string Target revision of the application source. cephClusters map Ceph clusters running on this cluster, keyed by FSID. The value is an unstructured object. conditions list Standard Kubernetes conditions. Types are listed below. observedGeneration integer Generation most recently observed. lastSync time Last time a sync was performed on the cluster. pxeSetupDone list of strings Hostnames already set up for PXE when talosManagementMode is Full.

kubectl get clusters prints topology, type, region, AZ, Superphenix version, Kubernetes version, node count, phase, and age.

items.title: Conditions
items.text: Type Reasons Reachable ConnectionSuccess, ConnectionFailed, SecretNotFound, InvalidSecret, ConnectionConfigError CompatibleVersion CompatibleVersion, IncompatibleVersion. InvalidVersion is used when a requested version change is invalid. ArgoCDSynced ArgoCDSynced, ArgoCDOutOfSync, ArgoCDSyncFailed, ArgoCDUnknown, ArgoCDSyncing Ready ReconcileSuccess, HealthCheckFailed, ApplicationReconcileFailed, AppProjectReconcileFailed, ConfigMapReconcileFailed, ConfigMapCleanupFailed, Deleting Paused Paused, Resumed

items.title: Example
items.text:
apiVersion: operator.superphenix.net/v1alpha1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: az-paris-1
  namespace: superphenix-system
spec:
  deploymentTopology: Decoupled
  type: Workload
  region: europe-west
  availabilityZone: paris-1
  connection:
    mode: Remote
    url: https://api.paris-1.example.net:6443
    secretRef:
      name: cluster-paris-1-credentials
  version: v0.1.0
  lifecycle:
    pause: false
    manual: false
    cleanupOnDeletion: false
  talosManagementMode: Unmanaged

items.title: Organization
items.text:
An Organization is a tenant organization onboarded through GitOps. It mirrors an organization created in the Superphenix console.

Group operator.superphenix.net Version v1alpha1 Kind Organization Plural organizations Scope Namespaced

Projects point at an Organization with spec.organizationRef. See Project.

items.title: Spec
items.text: Field Type Required Description organizationID string Yes Organization UUID issued by Superphenix. Must be a UUIDv4. name string No Overrides the organization name. When empty, the metadata name is used. At most 63 characters, and it must be a Kubernetes label value: letters, digits, -, _, and ., starting and ending with a letter or digit.

items.title: Status
items.text:
Field Type Description displayName string Effective name: spec.name when set, otherwise the metadata name. conditions list Standard Kubernetes conditions. observedGeneration integer Generation most recently observed.

kubectl get organizations prints the organization ID, display name, the Bound condition, and age.

items.title: Conditions
items.text: Type Reasons Meaning Bound Found The organization already exists in the Superphenix database. Bound Created The operator created the organization record. Bound Failed Binding the resource failed.

items.title: Example
items.text:
apiVersion: operator.superphenix.net/v1alpha1
kind: Organization
metadata:
  name: docs-demo-org
  namespace: superphenix-system
spec:
  organizationID: 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111
  name: docs-demo-org

items.title: Project
items.text:
A Project is a Superphenix project onboarded through GitOps. It belongs to one Organization and can be placed on one or more Cluster resources.

Group operator.superphenix.net Version v1alpha1 Kind Project Plural projects Scope Namespaced

items.title: Spec
items.text: Field Type Required Description projectID string Yes Project UUID issued by Superphenix. Must be a UUIDv4. name string No Overrides the project name. When empty, the metadata name is used. At most 63 characters, and it must be a Kubernetes label value. organizationRef object Yes Organization this project belongs to. See below. availabilityZones list No Clusters where this project may exist. See below. gitops object No Git repository overrides for this project's manifests and values. See below.

items.title: organizationRef
items.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes Name of the Organization resource. namespace string No Namespace of that Organization. Empty uses the Project's namespace.

items.title: availabilityZones[]
items.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes Name of the Cluster resource. namespace string No Namespace of that Cluster. Empty uses the Project's namespace.

items.title: gitops
items.text: Field Type Description manifestLocation.repoURL string Overrides the default repository URL for manifests. manifestLocation.path string Overrides the default manifest path. manifestLocation.targetRevision string Overrides the default manifest revision. valuesLocation.repoURL string Overrides the default repository URL for values. valuesLocation.path string Overrides the default values path. valuesLocation.targetRevision string Overrides the default values revision. valuesLocation.credentials.username string Username for the values repository. valuesLocation.credentials.password string Password for the values repository. Supply it from a secret store. Do not commit it. valuesLocation.credentials.insecure boolean Allow an insecure Git connection. valuesLocation.credentials.forceHttpBasicAuth boolean Force HTTP basic authentication. valuesLocation.credentials.enableLfs boolean Enable Git LFS. valuesLocation.credentials.sshPrivateKey string Private key for SSH authentication. Supply it from a secret store. Do not commit it.

items.title: Status
items.text:
Field Type Description displayName string Effective name: spec.name when set, otherwise the metadata name. availableZones list Availability zones where the project is available. availableZones[].name string Minimized name, region-az. availableZones[].clusterName string Full name of the cluster. availableAZsCount integer Number of available availability zones. conditions list Standard Kubernetes conditions. observedGeneration integer Generation most recently observed.

kubectl get projects prints the organization, project ID, display name, the Bound condition, the available AZ count, and age.

items.title: Conditions
items.text: Type Reasons Meaning Bound Found The project already exists in the Superphenix database. Bound Created The operator created the project record. Bound Failed Binding the resource failed. AvailabilityZonesReady Valid Every referenced availability zone is valid. AvailabilityZonesReady Invalid One or more availability zones are invalid.

items.title: Example
items.text:
apiVersion: operator.superphenix.net/v1alpha1
kind: Project
metadata:
  name: docs-demo-project
  namespace: superphenix-system
spec:
  projectID: 22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222
  name: docs-demo-project
  organizationRef:
    name: docs-demo-org
  availabilityZones:
    - name: az-paris-1
  gitops:
    manifestLocation:
      repoURL: https://github.com/example/project-manifests
      path: manifests
      targetRevision: main
    valuesLocation:
      repoURL: https://github.com/example/project-values
      path: values
      targetRevision: main

items.title: Helm charts
items.text:
Each page lists the chart's values and the documentation that ships with that chart in the Superphenix repository, under components/. A default is the chart default. Replace placeholder secrets before use. The pages call those placeholders out when the chart says they must be overridden.

The operator installs clusters by rendering superphenix-system. Per-cluster overrides go in Cluster.spec.systemConfiguration, documented on Cluster.

items.title: Platform
items.text:
These charts install the management plane and the stack on each cluster.

Chart Path What it configures superphenix-operator components/system/superphenix-operator Operator deployment, Argo CD, and the Cluster resources it manages. superphenix-system components/system/superphenix-system App-of-apps installed on management, hyperconverged, storage, and workload clusters. superphenix-api components/system/superphenix-api Superphenix API deployment. superphenix-controller components/system/superphenix-controller Per-AZ controller deployment.

items.title: Components
items.text:
The system chart renders these charts. Their values are what a cluster or a tenant project sets inside that app.

Chart Path What it configures sfs-iaas components/dependencies/sfs-iaas Tenant IaaS resources: VPCs, subnets, disks, and the rest of the self-service catalog. sfs-kaas components/dependencies/sfs-kaas Tenant Kubernetes clusters. sfs-baas components/dependencies/sfs-baas Backup policies. sfs-gitops components/dependencies/sfs-gitops GitOps identity for an organization and project. spx-policies components/dependencies/spx-policies Validating admission policies. spx-rook-connection components/dependencies/spx-rook-connection Connection from a workload cluster to a storage cluster. talos-manager components/dependencies/talos-manager PXE and Talos cluster configuration. Passed through Cluster.spec.talosManagerConfiguration. talos-backup components/dependencies/talos-backup Scheduled etcd backups. tuned components/dependencies/tuned Node tuning profiles. kaas-essentials components/dependencies/kaas-essentials Utilities inside a tenant cluster: HAProxy, Cilium, and KubeVirt CSI. kaas-datastore components/dependencies/kaas-datastore etcd datastores for Kamaji control planes. misc components/dependencies/misc Extra YAML objects selected by cluster mode.

items.title: Charts without values
items.text: These charts are bundled and installed by superphenix-system. Their values.yaml files are empty, so they have no operator-facing values of their own: cdi, csi-addons, external-snapshotter, kaas-controller, and multus.

items.title: kaas-datastore
items.text:
Values and chart documentation for components/dependencies/kaas-datastore in the Superphenix repository. Defaults are the chart defaults.

Deploys datastores (etcd clusters) for Kamaji controlplanes through etcd-operator.

items.title: Datastore default parameters
items.text: Key Type Default Description dataStoreDefaults object {"replicas":3,"storage":"10Gi"} Defines default values for datastores

items.title: Other Values
items.text: Key Type Default Description dataStores object {} Defines datastore resources for the controlplanes. Each key defines a datastore and should be unique See values.yaml for the complete syntax. location string ""

items.title: kaas-essentials

items.title: misc
items.text:
Values for components/dependencies/misc in the Superphenix repository. The chart deploys arbitrary YAML objects. superphenix-system passes effectiveMode so each object can be limited to a cluster mode.

Key Type Default Description effectiveMode string "" Effective mode of the cluster. Used to filter objects. modes object {} Map of object names to a list of modes. An object listed here is deployed only when effectiveMode is in its list. objects object {} YAML objects to deploy, keyed by name. The chart templates each object before applying it. 
objects:
  my-configmap:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: my-configmap
    data:
      key: "{{ .Release.Name }}"

items.title: Resource names
items.text:
Resources have a unique ID (see Creating new resources) and a name.

Names do not have to be unique across resources and can be identical. They are simply used as a tag to be filtered and found more easily.

To set a name on a resource, use the .name value.

items.title: sfs-iaas
items.text:
Values and chart documentation for components/dependencies/sfs-iaas in the Superphenix repository. Defaults are the chart defaults.

This Helm Chart is used by the self-service ArgoCDs of Superphenix to generate IaaS resources

items.title: Creating new resources
items.text:
For each type of resource present in this chart (VPC, Subnet, Disk, ...), there's a dictionary in which they can be created.

The key used to create a new resource within that dictionary is the ID of the resource.

Warning

This ID must be unique across resources of the same type within the project. If two resources of the same type have identical IDs, the one defined last in the dictionary will override all others.

For example, with a VPC:

vpcs:
  new-vpc: # This is the unique ID of the resource, no other VPC can have it
    name: "vpc"
    location: "aq01-test01"
  new-vpc: # WARNING: this key will override the one above
     name: "vpc2"
     location: "aq01-test01"

Note

IDs must begin with a letter or number, and may contain letters, numbers, hyphens, dots, and underscores, up to 63 characters each.

items.title: superphenix-operator
items.text: Values and chart documentation for components/system/superphenix-operator in the Superphenix repository. Defaults are the chart defaults.

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
The Superphenix Operator is the core component responsible for managing the lifecycle of Superphenix clusters.

  • Management Cluster Deployment: This operator is installed on the management cluster of SPX.
  • Cluster Lifecycle Management: It handles the installation and lifecycle management of Superphenix clusters using the Cluster Custom Resource Definition (CRD).
  • Deployment Engine: It deploys an ArgoCD instance as the deployment engine used to bootstrap all Superphenix clusters.
  • Self-Management: The management configuration (API, Console, etc.) is handled via the Helm chart, which deploys a Cluster resource pointing to the local Kubernetes cluster where the operator is running.
  • Versatility: The operator can be used to install various types of clusters, including hyperconverged or decoupled Availability Zones (AZs), storage clusters, and workload clusters.

items.title: Values
superphenix-system
items.text:
Values and chart documentation for components/system/superphenix-system in the Superphenix repository. Defaults are the chart defaults.

This chart is the central piece of the Superphenix system installation. It is responsible for installing and configuring all the necessary components on all Superphenix clusters, regardless of their role:

  • Management clusters: host the Superphenix control plane (console, API, identity, database, ...).
  • Hyperconverged clusters: combine storage and workload on the same nodes.
  • Storage clusters: dedicated to storage workloads (Rook / Ceph).
  • Workload clusters: dedicated to running virtualized workloads (KubeVirt).

While this chart could be used on its own, it is more likely to be used in conjunction with the Superphenix Operator. In a normal Superphenix deployment, the operator is responsible for installing clusters through this chart, by passing it the desired configuration.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
For every entry in .Values.apps the chart renders a single Argo CD Application object. Whether an entry actually results in an Application depends on three inputs:

  1. If the global switch .Values.disableAll is set to true, nothing is deployed.
  2. The per-app switch .Values.apps.<name>.enabled must be set to true.
  3. The per-app modes list must match against the effective mode of the target cluster.

The effective mode is the concatenation of .Values.cluster.deploymentTopology and .Values.cluster.type, giving one of:

deploymentTopology type Effective mode Hyperconverged (empty) Hyperconverged Decoupled Storage DecoupledStorage Decoupled Workload DecoupledWorkload (empty) Management Management
  • If an application's modes list is empty or not specified, it is considered eligible for deployment in any effective mode (as long as it is enabled).
  • If a list is provided, the application is deployed only if the cluster's effective mode is present in the list.

items.title: Global overrides
items.text:
A handful of top-level values act as blast-radius controls over every generated Application:

Field Effect disableAll Skip rendering every Application (useful for one-off maintenance). forceManual Force syncPolicy.automated.enabled = false on every Application, regardless of per-app automation.enabled. cleanupOnDeletion Add the resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io finalizer on every Application, forcing cascade delete.

items.title: Version parity
items.text: Applications that omit targetRevision (or set it to "") inherit Chart.AppVersion — the tag of this Git repository. That keeps every Superphenix-owned component in lockstep with the release of this chart.

items.title: Values
talos-backup
items.text:
Values and chart documentation for components/dependencies/talos-backup in the Superphenix repository. Defaults are the chart defaults.

Based on talos-backup :

talos-backup is a dead simple backup tool for Talos Linux-based Kubernetes clusters. The goal is simple: run this as a cronjob in a desire cluster, take an etcd snapshot, push said snapshot to s3.

Jobs run every day at 8:00 AM. Backups are compressed (with zstd) and encrypted (with age).

items.title: How to access backups
items.text:
# Store S3 credentials as environment variables
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID='***'
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='***'
export AWS_REGION='***'
export S3_ENDPOINT_URL='***'

# List files and directories
s5cmd ls s3://<bucket>/talos-backup/

# Copy file to working directory
s5cmd cp s3://<bucket>/talos-backup/<file> .

# Decrypt backup file with AGE secret key
age --decrypt -i <secret-key-txt-file> <file>.snap.zst.age > <file>.snap.zst

# Decompress decrypted file
zstd --decompress ./<file>.snap.zst
